        ("S008", "P006", "C005", "Clothing", "Jeans", 60.00, 1),
        ("S009", "P003", "C001", "Books", "Python Guide", 45.00, 2),
        ("S010", "P007", "C004", "Electronics", "Keyboard", 75.00, 1),
    ]
    
    sales_schema = StructType([
        StructField("sale_id", StringType(), False),
        StructField("product_id", StringType(), False),
        StructField("customer_id", StringType(), False),
        StructField("category", StringType(), False),
        StructField("product_name", StringType(), False),
        StructField("price", DoubleType(), False),
        StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), False)
    ])
    
    sales_df = spark.createDataFrame(sales_data, sales_schema)
    
    # Customer data
    customer_data = [
        ("C001", "John Doe", "john@email.com", "New York"),
        ("C002", "Jane Smith", "jane@email.com", "Los Angeles"),
        ("C003", "Bob Johnson", "bob@email.com", "Chicago"),
        ("C004", "Alice Brown", "alice@email.com", "Houston"),
        ("C005", "Charlie Wilson", "charlie@email.com", "Phoenix"),
    ]
    
    customer_schema = StructType([
        StructField("customer_id", StringType(), False),
        StructField("name", StringType(), False),
        StructField("email", StringType(), False),
        StructField("city", StringType(), False)
    ])
    
    customers_df = spark.createDataFrame(customer_data, customer_schema)
    
    return sales_df, customers_df


# ============================================================================
# Pattern 1: Collect List Pattern
# ============================================================================

def collect_list_pattern(sales_df):
    """
    Collect List Pattern: Aggregates values into a list, preserving duplicates.
    
    Use Case: When you need to maintain all occurrences of values,
    including duplicates, in a specific order.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("1. COLLECT LIST PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Aggregate values into a list, preserving duplicates")
    print()
    
    # Example 1: Collect all products purchased by each customer
    customer_products = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_name").alias("products_list"),
            collect_list("price").alias("prices_list")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id")
    
    print("Products purchased by each customer (with duplicates):")
    customer_products.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Collect sales by category with order preservation
    category_sales = sales_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(struct("sale_id", "product_name", "price")).alias("sales_details")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nSales details by category:")
    category_sales.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 3: Collect with ordering
    ordered_collection = sales_df.orderBy(desc("price")) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_name").alias("products_by_price_desc")
        )
    
    print("\nProducts by category ordered by price (descending):")
    ordered_collection.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Pattern 2: Collect Set Pattern
# ============================================================================

def collect_set_pattern(sales_df):
    """
    Collect Set Pattern: Aggregates unique values into a set.
    
    Use Case: When you need only distinct values without duplicates.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("2. COLLECT SET PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Aggregate unique values into a set (no duplicates)")
    print()
    
    # Example 1: Unique products per customer
    unique_customer_products = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            collect_set("product_name").alias("unique_products"),
            collect_set("category").alias("categories_shopped")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id")
    
    print("Unique products and categories per customer:")
    unique_customer_products.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Unique customers per category
    unique_category_customers = sales_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_set("customer_id").alias("unique_customers"),
            collect_set("product_name").alias("unique_products")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nUnique customers and products per category:")
    unique_category_customers.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 3: Compare list vs set
    comparison = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_name").alias("all_products"),
            collect_set("product_name").alias("unique_products"),
            size(collect_list("product_name")).alias("total_purchases"),
            size(collect_set("product_name")).alias("unique_purchases")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id")
    
    print("\nComparison: List vs Set collection:")
    comparison.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Pattern 3: Collect Map Pattern
# ============================================================================

def collect_map_pattern(sales_df):
    """
    Collect Map Pattern: Aggregates key-value pairs into a map/dictionary.
    
    Use Case: When you need to create lookup structures or 
    associate related values.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("3. COLLECT MAP PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Aggregate key-value pairs into a map structure")
    print()
    
    # Example 1: Create product-to-price mapping per customer
    product_price_map = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(struct("product_name", "price"))
            ).alias("product_price_map")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id")
    
    print("Product-to-Price mapping per customer:")
    product_price_map.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Create product-to-quantity mapping
    product_quantity_map = sales_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            map_from_entries(
                collect_list(struct("product_id", "quantity"))
            ).alias("product_quantities")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nProduct-to-Quantity mapping per category:")
    product_quantity_map.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 3: Complex nested map
    customer_category_map = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(
                    struct(
                        col("category"),
                        struct("product_name", "price", "quantity").alias("details")
                    )
                )
            ).alias("category_details_map")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id")
    
    print("\nCategory-to-Details mapping per customer:")
    customer_category_map.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Pattern 4: Top-N Collection Pattern
# ============================================================================

def top_n_collection_pattern(sales_df):
    """
    Top-N Collection Pattern: Collects only the top N items based on criteria.
    
    Use Case: When you need to retrieve the best/worst performing items,
    highest/lowest values, etc.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("4. TOP-N COLLECTION PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Collect only the top N items based on specific criteria")
    print()
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    # Example 1: Top 3 most expensive products per category
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(desc("price"))
    
    top_products_per_category = sales_df \
        .withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .filter(col("rank") <= 3) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(
                struct("rank", "product_name", "price")
            ).alias("top_3_products")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("Top 3 most expensive products per category:")
    top_products_per_category.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Top 2 customers by total spending
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum, row_number
    
    customer_spending = sales_df \
        .withColumn("total_amount", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(_sum("total_amount").alias("total_spent"))
    
    window_customer = Window.orderBy(desc("total_spent"))
    
    top_customers = customer_spending \
        .withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window_customer)) \
        .filter(col("rank") <= 2) \
        .select("customer_id", "total_spent", "rank")
    
    print("\nTop 2 customers by spending:")
    top_customers.show()
    
    # Example 3: Using array slice for top N
    top_n_using_slice = sales_df.orderBy(desc("price")) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            slice(
                collect_list(struct("product_name", "price")),
                1,  # start position (1-indexed)
                3   # length
            ).alias("top_3_by_price")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nTop 3 products using array slice:")
    top_n_using_slice.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Pattern 5: Sample Collection Pattern
# ============================================================================

def sample_collection_pattern(sales_df):
    """
    Sample Collection Pattern: Collects a random sample of data.
    
    Use Case: When you need representative samples for analysis,
    testing, or preview purposes.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("5. SAMPLE COLLECTION PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Collect random samples of data")
    print()
    
    # Example 1: Random sample of entire dataset
    sample_fraction = 0.5  # 50% sample
    random_sample = sales_df.sample(
        withReplacement=False,
        fraction=sample_fraction,
        seed=42
    )
    
    print(f"Random sample ({sample_fraction*100}% of data):")
    random_sample.show()
    print(f"Original count: {sales_df.count()}, Sample count: {random_sample.count()}")
    
    # Example 2: Stratified sampling by category
    # Get proportional samples from each category
    category_fractions = {
        "Electronics": 0.6,
        "Books": 0.5,
        "Clothing": 0.7
    }
    
    stratified_sample = sales_df.sampleBy(
        col="category",
        fractions=category_fractions,
        seed=42
    )
    
    print("\nStratified sample by category:")
    stratified_sample.groupBy("category").count().show()
    
    # Example 3: Random N items per group
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    from pyspark.sql.functions import row_number
    
    # Add random ordering and select top 2 per category
    window_random = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(rand(seed=42))
    
    random_per_group = sales_df \
        .withColumn("random_rank", row_number().over(window_random)) \
        .filter(col("random_rank") <= 2) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(
                struct("product_name", "price")
            ).alias("random_samples")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nRandom 2 items per category:")
    random_per_group.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 4: Reservoir sampling simulation
    # Collect random sample with limit
    reservoir_size = 5
    reservoir_sample = sales_df \
        .orderBy(rand(seed=42)) \
        .limit(reservoir_size)
    
    print(f"\nReservoir sample (n={reservoir_size}):")
    reservoir_sample.show()


# ============================================================================
# Pattern 6: Limited Collection Pattern
# ============================================================================

def limited_collection_pattern(sales_df):
    """
    Limited Collection Pattern: Collects data with size constraints.
    
    Use Case
```python
    """
    Limited Collection Pattern: Collects data with size constraints.
    
    Use Case: When you need to limit collection size for memory management,
    performance optimization, or preview purposes.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("6. LIMITED COLLECTION PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Collect data with size constraints and limits")
    print()
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import slice, size, array_sort
    
    # Example 1: Limit number of items collected per group
    max_items = 2
    limited_products = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            slice(
                collect_list("product_name"),
                1,
                max_items
            ).alias("limited_products")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id")
    
    print(f"Limited to {max_items} products per customer:")
    limited_products.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Conditional collection with size limit
    # Collect products but limit array size
    conditional_limited = sales_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_name").alias("all_products"),
            slice(collect_list("product_name"), 1, 3).alias("first_3_products"),
            size(collect_list("product_name")).alias("total_count")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nConditional limited collection:")
    conditional_limited.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 3: Limited collection with head/take
    print("\nUsing take() to limit collection:")
    limited_rows = sales_df.orderBy(desc("price")).take(5)
    
    print(f"Top 5 most expensive items (using take):")
    for idx, row in enumerate(limited_rows, 1):
        print(f"{idx}. {row['product_name']}: ${row['price']:.2f}")
    
    # Example 4: First N and Last N pattern
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    from pyspark.sql.functions import row_number, count
    
    # Get first 2 and last 2 sales per category
    window_asc = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(asc("sale_id"))
    window_desc = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(desc("sale_id"))
    
    first_last_sales = sales_df \
        .withColumn("rank_asc", row_number().over(window_asc)) \
        .withColumn("rank_desc", row_number().over(window_desc)) \
        .filter((col("rank_asc") <= 2) | (col("rank_desc") <= 2)) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(
                struct("sale_id", "product_name", "rank_asc", "rank_desc")
            ).alias("first_and_last_sales")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nFirst and last sales per category:")
    first_last_sales.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 5: Paginated collection pattern
    page_size = 3
    page_number = 1  # 0-indexed
    
    paginated_data = sales_df \
        .orderBy("sale_id") \
        .limit(page_size) \
        .offset(page_number * page_size)
    
    print(f"\nPaginated collection (page {page_number + 1}, size {page_size}):")
    paginated_data.show()
    
    # Example 6: Collect with memory-safe limit
    # Using limit before collect to prevent OOM
    safe_collect_limit = 100
    
    safe_collection = sales_df \
        .orderBy(desc("price")) \
        .limit(safe_collect_limit) \
        .collect()
    
    print(f"\nSafe collection with limit={safe_collect_limit}:")
    print(f"Collected {len(safe_collection)} rows safely")
    
    # Example 7: Bounded collection per group
    from pyspark.sql.functions import expr
    
    bounded_per_group = sales_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_name").alias("all_products")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "bounded_products",
            expr("slice(all_products, 1, 2)")  # Limit to first 2
        ) \
        .withColumn("product_count", size(col("all_products"))) \
        .select("category", "bounded_products", "product_count") \
        .orderBy("category")
    
    print("\nBounded collection per group:")
    bounded_per_group.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Advanced Pattern: Combined Collection Patterns
# ============================================================================

def combined_collection_patterns(sales_df, customers_df):
    """
    Demonstrates combining multiple collection patterns for complex use cases.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
        customers_df: Customers DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED: COMBINED COLLECTION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Purpose: Combine multiple patterns for complex analytics")
    print()
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        sum as _sum, avg, max as _max, min as _min,
        count, row_number, dense_rank
    )
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    # Example 1: Top customers with their product preferences
    # Combines: Top-N, Collect Set, and Limited patterns
    
    customer_analysis = sales_df \
        .withColumn("total_amount", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            _sum("total_amount").alias("total_spent"),
            collect_set("category").alias("categories"),
            collect_list("product_name").alias("all_products"),
            slice(
                array_sort(collect_set("product_name")),
                1,
                5
            ).alias("top_5_unique_products"),
            count("*").alias("purchase_count")
        )
    
    window_spending = Window.orderBy(desc("total_spent"))
    
    top_customer_analysis = customer_analysis \
        .withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window_spending)) \
        .filter(col("rank") <= 3) \
        .join(customers_df, "customer_id") \
        .select(
            "rank",
            "customer_id",
            "name",
            "total_spent",
            "purchase_count",
            "categories",
            "top_5_unique_products"
        ) \
        .orderBy("rank")
    
    print("Top 3 customers with detailed analysis:")
    top_customer_analysis.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Category performance with sample products
    # Combines: Collect Map, Sample, and Aggregate patterns
    
    category_performance = sales_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            _sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("price").alias("avg_price"),
            count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
            collect_set("product_name").alias("unique_products"),
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(struct("product_name", "price"))
            ).alias("product_price_catalog"),
            slice(
                collect_list(struct("product_name", "revenue")),
                1,
                3
            ).alias("sample_transactions")
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
    
    print("\nCategory performance with samples:")
    category_performance.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 3: Customer segmentation with limited details
    # Combines: Collect List, Limited, and Conditional patterns
    
    customer_segments = sales_df \
        .withColumn("total_amount", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            _sum("total_amount").alias("lifetime_value"),
            count("*").alias("purchase_frequency"),
            collect_set("category").alias("category_preferences"),
            slice(
                collect_list(
                    struct("sale_id", "product_name", "price")
                ),
                1,
                3
            ).alias("recent_purchases_sample")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "segment",
            expr("""
                CASE 
                    WHEN lifetime_value > 2000 THEN 'Premium'
                    WHEN lifetime_value > 1000 THEN 'Standard'
                    ELSE 'Basic'
                END
            """)
        ) \
        .join(customers_df, "customer_id") \
        .select(
            "customer_id",
            "name",
            "segment",
            "lifetime_value",
            "purchase_frequency",
            "category_preferences",
            "recent_purchases_sample"
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("lifetime_value"))
    
    print("\nCustomer segmentation analysis:")
    customer_segments.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Performance Optimization Tips
# ============================================================================

def performance_tips():
    """
    Displays best practices and performance tips for collection patterns.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION TIPS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    tips = """
    1. COLLECT LIST vs COLLECT SET:
       - Use collect_set when duplicates don't matter (more efficient)
       - Use collect_list when order and duplicates are important
       - collect_set requires less memory
    
    2. LIMIT COLLECTION SIZE:
       - Always use limits when collecting large datasets
       - Use slice() or take() to prevent OOM errors
       - Consider using approx_count_distinct for large cardinality
    
    3. AVOID COLLECT() ON LARGE DATASETS:
       - collect() brings all data to driver memory
       - Use take(n) instead of collect() when possible
       - Use show() for preview instead of collect()
    
    4. OPTIMIZE GROUPBY OPERATIONS:
       - Partition data appropriately before groupBy
       - Use broadcast joins for small lookup tables
       - Consider using reduceByKey for simple aggregations
    
    5. SAMPLING STRATEGIES:
       - Use sampleBy() for stratified sampling
       - Set appropriate seed for reproducibility
       - Use reservoir sampling for streaming data
    
    6. MEMORY MANAGEMENT:
       - Monitor executor memory when collecting
       - Use persist() for reused collections
       - Clear cache when collections are no longer needed
    
    7. TOP-N OPTIMIZATION:
       - Use window functions with LIMIT instead of sorting entire dataset
       - Consider using approx_percentile for approximate results
       - Partition data to parallelize top-N operations
    
    8. MAP COLLECTIONS:
       - Use map_from_entries for key-value pairs
       - Ensure keys are unique to avoid data loss
       - Consider nested structures for complex relationships
    """
    
    print(tips)

# Main Execution
# ============================================================================

def main():
    """
    Main execution function that demonstrates all collection patterns.
    """
    try:
        # Create sample data
        sales_df, customers_df = create_sample_data()
        
        print("\nSample Data Overview:")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("Sales Data:")
        sales_df.show(5)
        
        print("Customers Data:")
        customers_df.show()
        
        # Execute all patterns
        collect_list_pattern(sales_df)
        collect_set_pattern(sales_df)
        collect_map_pattern(sales_df)
        top_n_collection_pattern(sales_df)
        sample_collection_pattern(sales_df)
        limited_collection_pattern(sales_df)
        
        # Advanced combined patterns
        combined_collection_patterns(sales_df, customers_df)
        
        # Display performance tips
        performance_tips()
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("SUMMARY OF COLLECTION PATTERNS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        summary = """
        Pattern                 | Use Case                          | Key Function
        ------------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------
        Collect List           | Preserve all values + duplicates  | collect_list()
        Collect Set            | Unique values only                | collect_set()
        Collect Map            | Key-value pair aggregation        | map_from_entries()
        Top-N Collection       | Best/worst N items                | Window + slice()
        Sample Collection      | Random representative samples     | sample()/sampleBy()
        Limited Collection     | Size-constrained collection       | limit()/take()
        """
        
        print(summary)
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("Demo completed successfully!")
        print("=" * 80)
        
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"\nError occurred: {str(e)}")
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()
    
    finally:
        # Clean up
        print("\nCleaning up Spark session...")
        spark.stop()
        print("Spark session stopped.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# ============================================================================
# Bonus: Utility Functions for Collection Patterns

def collection_pattern_utilities():
    """
    Additional utility functions for working with collection patterns.
    """
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        explode, posexplode, arrays_zip, transform,
        filter as array_filter, aggregate, exists
    )
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("BONUS: COLLECTION PATTERN UTILITIES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Sample data for utilities
    data = [
        ("A", [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]),
        ("B", [2, 4, 6, 8]),
        ("C", [1, 3, 5, 7, 9])
    ]
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "numbers"])
    
    # Utility 1: Explode collections
    print("\n1. Explode Collection:")
    df.select("id", explode("numbers").alias("number")).show()
    
    # Utility 2: Position explode
    print("2. Position Explode:")
    df.select("id", posexplode("numbers")).show()
    
    # Utility 3: Array transformation
    print("3. Transform Array Elements:")
    df.withColumn(
        "doubled",
        transform(col("numbers"), lambda x: x * 2)
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Utility 4: Filter arrays
    print("4. Filter Array Elements:")
    df.withColumn(
        "even_numbers",
        array_filter(col("numbers"), lambda x: x % 2 == 0)
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Utility 5: Check existence
    print("5. Check Element Existence:")
    df.withColumn(
        "has_five",
        exists(col("numbers"), lambda x: x == 5)
    ).show()
```

# ============================================================================

def run_specific_pattern_examples():
    """
    Demonstrates how to use each pattern independently with real-world scenarios.
    """
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("REAL-WORLD USAGE EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Initialize data
    sales_df, customers_df = create_sample_data()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Use Case 1: E-commerce Order History
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n📦 Use Case 1: E-commerce Order History")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    order_history = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            # All orders (with duplicates for repeat purchases)
            collect_list("product_name").alias("order_history"),
            # Unique products ever purchased
            collect_set("product_name").alias("unique_products_purchased"),
            # Product catalog with prices
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(struct("product_name", "price"))
            ).alias("product_price_reference"),
            # Total metrics
            count("*").alias("total_orders"),
            _sum(col("price") * col("quantity")).alias("lifetime_value")
        ) \
        .join(customers_df, "customer_id") \
        .select(
            "customer_id",
            "name",
            "order_history",
            "unique_products_purchased",
            "total_orders",
            "lifetime_value"
        )
    
    print("Customer Order History:")
    order_history.show(truncate=False)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Use Case 2: Product Recommendation System
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n🎯 Use Case 2: Product Recommendation System")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    # Find frequently bought together products
    product_associations = sales_df.alias("s1") \
        .join(
            sales_df.alias("s2"),
            (col("s1.customer_id") == col("s2.customer_id")) &
            (col("s1.product_id") != col("s2.product_id"))
        ) \
        .groupBy(col("s1.product_name").alias("product")) \
        .agg(
            collect_list(col("s2.product_name")).alias("bought_together"),
            count("*").alias("co_occurrence_count")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "top_recommendations",
            slice(
                collect_set(col("bought_together")).over(
                    Window.partitionBy("product").orderBy(desc("co_occurrence_count"))
                ),
                1,
                3
            )
        )
    
    print("Product Recommendations (Frequently Bought Together):")
    product_associations.select("product", "top_recommendations").distinct().show(truncate=False)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Use Case 3: Inventory Management Dashboard
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n📊 Use Case 3: Inventory Management Dashboard")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    inventory_summary = sales_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            # Total products in category
            collect_set("product_name").alias("all_products"),
            # Sample products for quick view
            slice(collect_set("product_name"), 1, 3).alias("sample_products"),
            # Sales statistics
            _sum(col("quantity")).alias("total_units_sold"),
            _sum(col("price") * col("quantity")).alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("price").alias("avg_price"),
            # Price range
            _min("price").alias("min_price"),
            _max("price").alias("max_price"),
            # Count metrics
            size(collect_set("product_name")).alias("unique_product_count"),
            count("*").alias("transaction_count")
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
    
    print("Inventory Dashboard by Category:")
    inventory_summary.show(truncate=False)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Use Case 4: Customer Segmentation for Marketing
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n📈 Use Case 4: Customer Segmentation for Marketing")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    customer_segments = sales_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            _sum("revenue").alias("total_spent"),
            count("*").alias("purchase_count"),
            avg("revenue").alias("avg_order_value"),
            collect_set("category").alias("categories_purchased"),
            size(collect_set("category")).alias("category_diversity"),
            # Recent purchases (limited to last 3)
            slice(
                collect_list(struct("product_name", "price", "quantity")),
                1,
                3
            ).alias("recent_purchases")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "customer_segment",
            expr("""
                CASE
                    WHEN total_spent > 2000 AND category_diversity >= 2 THEN 'VIP Multi-Category'
                    WHEN total_spent > 2000 THEN 'VIP Single-Category'
                    WHEN total_spent > 500 AND purchase_count >= 3 THEN 'Loyal'
                    WHEN purchase_count >= 3 THEN 'Frequent'
                    ELSE 'Casual'
                END
            """)
        ) \
        .join(customers_df, "customer_id") \
        .select(
            "customer_id",
            "name",
            "customer_segment",
            "total_spent",
            "purchase_count",
            "avg_order_value",
            "categories_purchased",
            "recent_purchases"
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_spent"))
    
    print("Customer Segmentation:")
    customer_segments.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Segment distribution
    print("\nSegment Distribution:")
    customer_segments.groupBy("customer_segment") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("customer_count"),
            avg("total_spent").alias("avg_lifetime_value")
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("avg_lifetime_value")) \
        .show()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Use Case 5: Sales Performance Analytics
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n💰 Use Case 5: Sales Performance Analytics")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import percentile_approx
    
    sales_analytics = sales_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            # Revenue metrics
            _sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("revenue").alias("avg_revenue"),
            percentile_approx("revenue", 0.5).alias("median_revenue"),
            # Top performers
            slice(
                array_sort(
                    collect_list(struct(col("revenue"), col("product_name"))),
                    lambda x: x.revenue.desc()
                ),
                1,
                3
            ).alias("top_3_revenue_products"),
            # Product diversity
            size(collect_set("product_name")).alias("product_count"),
            # Transaction patterns
            collect_list("quantity").alias("quantity_distribution"),
            avg("quantity").alias("avg_quantity_per_sale")
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
    
    print("Sales Performance by Category:")
    sales_analytics.show(truncate=False)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Use Case 6: A/B Testing Sample Selection
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n🧪 Use Case 6: A/B Testing Sample Selection")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    # Stratified sampling for A/B test groups
    test_group_fractions = {
        "Electronics": 0.5,
        "Books": 0.5,
        "Clothing": 0.5
    }
    
    ab_test_sample = sales_df.sampleBy(
        col="category",
        fractions=test_group_fractions,
        seed=42
    ).withColumn("test_group", expr("'A'"))
    
    # Get complementary sample for group B
    ab_test_ids = ab_test_sample.select("sale_id").collect()
    ab_test_id_list = [row.sale_id for row in ab_test_ids]
    
    group_b = sales_df.filter(~col("sale_id").isin(ab_test_id_list)) \
        .withColumn("test_group", expr("'B'"))
    
    # Combine both groups
    ab_test_full = ab_test_sample.union(group_b)
    
    print("A/B Test Group Distribution:")
    ab_test_full.groupBy("test_group", "category") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("sample_size"),
            _sum(col("price") * col("quantity")).alias("total_revenue")
        ) \
        .orderBy("category", "test_group") \
        .show()


# ============================================================================
# Advanced Pattern: Windowed Collections
# ============================================================================

def windowed_collection_patterns(sales_df):
    """
    Demonstrates collection patterns with window functions for time-series
    and sequential data analysis.
    
    Args:
        sales_df: Sales DataFrame
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED: WINDOWED COLLECTION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    from pyspark.sql.functions import lag, lead, row_number
    
    # Add timestamp for demonstration
    sales_with_time = sales_df.withColumn(
        "sale_date",
        expr("date_add('2024-01-01', cast(substring(sale_id, 2) as int))")
    )
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Pattern 1: Running Collection (Cumulative)
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n1. Running/Cumulative Collection Pattern:")
    
    window_running = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("sale_date") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    running_collection = sales_with_time \
        .withColumn(
            "cumulative_products",
            collect_list("product_name").over(window_running)
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "cumulative_spending",
            _sum(col("price") * col("quantity")).over(window_running)
        ) \
        .select(
            "customer_id",
            "sale_date",
            "product_name",
            "cumulative_products",
            "cumulative_spending"
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id", "sale_date")
    
    print("Cumulative product collection per customer:")
    running_collection.show(truncate=False)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Pattern 2: Sliding Window Collection
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n2. Sliding Window Collection Pattern:")
    
    window_sliding = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy("sale_date") \
        .rowsBetween(-2, 0)  # Current row and 2 preceding rows
    
    sliding_collection = sales_with_time \
        .withColumn(
            "last_3_products",
            collect_list("product_name").over(window_sliding)
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "last_3_avg_price",
            avg("price").over(window_sliding)
        ) \
        .select(
            "category",
            "sale_date",
            "product_name",
            "price",
            "last_3_products",
            "last_3_avg_price"
        ) \
        .orderBy("category", "sale_date")
    
    print("Sliding window (last 3) collection:")
    sliding_collection.show(truncate=False)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Pattern 3: Lead/Lag Collection Pattern
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n3. Lead/Lag Collection Pattern:")
    
    window_seq = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("sale_date")
    
    lead_lag_pattern = sales_with_time \
        .withColumn("previous_product", lag("product_name", 1).over(window_seq)) \
        .withColumn("next_product", lead("product_name", 1).over(window_seq)) \
        .withColumn(
            "purchase_sequence",
            array(
                col("previous_product"),
                col("product_name"),
                col("next_product")
            )
        ) \
        .select(
            "customer_id",
            "sale_date",
            "product_name",
            "purchase_sequence"
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id", "sale_date")
    
    print("Purchase sequence with lead/lag:")
    lead_lag_pattern.show(truncate=False)

# ============================================================================
# Error Handling and Edge Cases
# ============================================================================

def handle_edge_cases():
    """
    Demonstrates proper error handling and edge case management
    for collection patterns.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ERROR HANDLING AND EDGE CASES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Edge Case 1: Empty collections
    print("\n1. Handling Empty Collections:")
    empty_data = spark.createDataFrame([], "id STRING, value INT")
    
    try:
        result = empty_data.groupBy("id").agg(collect_list("value").alias("values"))
        print("Empty collection result:")
        result.show()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error: {e}")
    
    # Edge Case 2: Null values in collections
    print("\n2. Handling Null Values:")
    null_data = [
        ("A", 1),
        ("A", None),
        ("A", 3),
        ("B", None),
        ("B", 2)
    ]
    null_df = spark.createDataFrame(null_data, ["id", "value"])
    
    # Collect with nulls
    null_collection = null_df.groupBy("id").agg(
        collect_list("value").alias("with_nulls"),
        collect_set("value").alias("set_with_nulls"),
        # Filter out nulls
        array_filter(collect_list("value"), lambda x: x.isNotNull()).alias("without_nulls")
    )
    
    print("Collection with null handling:")
    null_collection.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Edge Case 3: Very large collections (memory safety)
    print("\n3. Memory-Safe Large Collections:")
    
    def safe_collect_pattern(df, group_col, collect_col, max_items=1000):
        """
        Safely collect data with size limits to prevent OOM errors.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            group_col: Column to group by
            collect_col: Column to collect
            max_items: Maximum items to collect per group
            
        Returns:
            DataFrame with limited collections
        """
        from pyspark.sql.window import Window
        
        # Add row number within each group
        window = Window.partitionBy(group_col).orderBy(collect_col)
        
        limited_df = df \
            .withColumn("_row_num", row_number().over(window)) \
            .filter(col("_row_num") <= max_items) \
            .groupBy(group_col) \
            .agg(
                collect_list(collect_col).alias(f"{collect_col}_list"),
                count("*").alias("collection_size")
            )
        
        return limited_df
    
    # Test with sample data
    test_data = [(f"Group{i%3}", f"Value{j}") 
                 for i in range(3) for j in range(100)]
    test_df = spark.createDataFrame(test_data, ["group", "value"])
    
    safe_result = safe_collect_pattern(test_df, "group", "value", max_items=10)
    print("Safe collection with size limit:")
    safe_result.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Edge Case 4: Duplicate keys in map collections
    print("\n4. Handling Duplicate Keys in Maps:")
    dup_data = [
        ("A", "key1", "value1"),
        ("A", "key1", "value2"),  # Duplicate key
        ("A", "key2", "value3")
    ]
    dup_df = spark.createDataFrame(dup_data, ["id", "key", "value"])
    
    # Last value wins in map_from_entries
    map_result = dup_df.groupBy("id").agg(
        map_from_entries(collect_list(struct("key", "value"))).alias("map_last_wins"),
        map_from_entries(collect_set(struct("key", "value"))).alias("map_with_set")
    )
    
    print("Map with duplicate keys (last value wins):")
    map_result.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Edge Case 5: Empty groups after filtering
    print("\n5. Handling Empty Groups After Filtering:")
    filter_data = [
        ("A", 5),
        ("A", 15),
        ("B", 3),
        ("C", 25)
    ]
    filter_df = spark.createDataFrame(filter_data, ["group", "value"])
    
    # Filter and collect
    filtered_collection = filter_df \
        .filter(col("value") > 10) \
        .groupBy("group") \
        .agg(collect_list("value").alias("values"))
    
    print("Collection after filtering (some groups may be missing):")
    filtered_collection.show()
    
    # To preserve all groups with empty collections
    all_groups = filter_df.select("group").distinct()
    complete_result = all_groups.join(
        filtered_collection,
        "group",
        "left"
    ).fillna({"values": []})
    
    print("Preserving all groups with empty collections:")
    complete_result.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Export and Persistence Patterns
# ============================================================================

def export_collection_patterns():
    """
    Demonstrates how to export and persist collection results.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("EXPORT AND PERSISTENCE PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    sales_df, customers_df = create_sample_data()
    
    # Pattern 1: Export to JSON (preserves complex structures)
    print("\n1. Export Collections to JSON:")
    
    json_export = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
        collect_list(
            struct("product_name", "price", "quantity")
        ).alias("purchases")
    )
    
    # Write to JSON
    output_path = "/tmp/customer_purchases_json"
    try:
        json_export.write.mode("overwrite").json(output_path)
        print(f"✓ Exported to JSON: {output_path}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Note: {e}")
    
    # Pattern 2: Export to Parquet (efficient storage)
    print("\n2. Export Collections to Parquet:")
    
    parquet_export = sales_df.groupBy("category").agg(
        collect_set("product_name").alias("products"),
        collect_list(struct("customer_id", "quantity")).alias("sales")
    )
    
    output_path = "/tmp/category_collections_parquet"
    try:
        parquet_export.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(output_path)
        print(f"✓ Exported to Parquet: {output_path}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Note: {e}")
    
    # Pattern 3: Convert to Pandas for local analysis
    print("\n3. Convert to Pandas DataFrame:")
    
    pandas_export = sales_df.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
        collect_list("product_name").alias("products")
    ).limit(5)  # Limit for safety
    
    try:
        pandas_df = pandas_export.toPandas()
        print("✓ Converted to Pandas:")
        print(pandas_df)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error: {e}")
    
    # Pattern 4: Persist for reuse
    print("\n4. Caching Collections for Reuse:")
    
    cached_collection = sales_df.groupBy("category").agg(
        collect_list("product_name").alias("products")
    ).cache()
    
    print(f"Collection cached: {cached_collection.is_cached}")
    
    # Use multiple times
    print("First use:")
    cached_collection.show()
    
    print("Second use (from cache):")
    cached_collection.count()
    
    # Clean up cache
    cached_collection.unpersist()
    print("Cache cleared")


# ============================================================================
# Complete Integration Example
# ============================================================================

def complete_integration_example():
    """
    A complete real-world example integrating multiple collection patterns
    for a comprehensive analytics pipeline.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("COMPLETE INTEGRATION EXAMPLE: E-COMMERCE ANALYTICS PIPELINE")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    sales_df, customers_df = create_sample_data()
    
    # Step 1: Customer 360 View
    print("\n📊 Step 1: Building Customer 360 View")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    customer_360 = sales_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            # Financial metrics
            _sum("revenue").alias("lifetime_value"),
            avg("revenue").alias("avg_order_value"),
            count("*").alias("total_orders"),
            
            # Product preferences
            collect_set("category").alias("categories_purchased"),
            collect_set("product_name").alias("unique_products"),
            
            # Purchase history (limited)
            slice(
                collect_list(
                    struct("product_name", "price", "quantity", "revenue")
                ),
                1,
                10
            ).alias("recent_purchases"),
            
            # Product-price catalog for this customer
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(struct("product_name", "price"))
            ).alias("product_price_catalog"),
            
            # Category spending breakdown
            map_from_entries(
                collect_list(
                    struct("category", "revenue")
                )
            ).alias("category_spending")
        ) \
        .join(customers_df, "customer_id") \
        .select(
            "customer_id",
            "name",
            "email",
            "city",
            "lifetime_value",
            "avg_order_value",
            "total_orders",
            "categories_purchased",
            "unique_products",
            "recent_purchases",
            "category_spending"
        )
    
    print("Customer 360 View:")
    customer_360.show(2, truncate=False)
    
    # Step 2: Product Performance Analysis
    print("\n📦 Step 2: Product Performance Analysis")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    product_performance = sales_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("product_name", "category") \
        .agg(
            _sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
            _sum("quantity").alias("total_units_sold"),
            count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
            collect_set("customer_id").alias("unique_customers"),
            size(collect_set("customer_id")).alias("customer_reach"),
            avg("quantity").alias("avg_quantity_per_order")
        )
    
    # Rank products within categories
    window_category = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
    
    ranked_products = product_performance \
        .withColumn("category_rank", row_number().over(window_category)) \
        .orderBy("category", "category_rank")
    
    print("Top Products by Category:")
    ranked_products.filter(col("category_rank") <= 2).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Step 3: Market Basket Analysis
    print("\n🛒 Step 3: Market Basket Analysis")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    # Find product combinations purchased together
    basket_analysis = sales_df.alias("s1") \
        .join(
            sales_df.alias("s2"),
            (col("s1.customer_id") == col("s2.customer_id")) &
            (col("s1.product_name") < col("s2.product_name"))  # Avoid duplicates
        ) \
        .groupBy(
            col("s1.product_name").alias("product_a"),
            col("s2.product_name").alias("product_b")
        ) \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("co_purchase_count"),
            collect_set(col("s1.customer_id")).alias("customers")
        ) \
        .filter(col("co_purchase_count") >= 2) \
        .orderBy(desc("co_purchase_count"))
    
    print("Frequently Bought Together:")
    basket_analysis.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Step 4: Customer Segmentation with Recommendations
    print("\n🎯 Step 4: Customer Segmentation with Recommendations")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    # Segment customers and provide recommendations
    customer_segments_detailed = customer_360 \
        .withColumn(
            "segment",
            expr("""
                CASE
                    WHEN lifetime_value > 2000 THEN 'Premium'
                    WHEN lifetime_value > 1000 THEN 'Gold'
                    WHEN total_orders >= 3 THEN 'Silver'
                    ELSE 'Bronze'
                END
            """)
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "category_count",

def test_collection_patterns():
    """
    Unit tests for collection patterns to ensure correctness.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("TESTING COLLECTION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Test data
    test_data = [
        ("A", "item1", 10),
        ("A", "item2", 20),
        ("A", "item1", 10),  # Duplicate
        ("B", "item3", 30),
    ]
    test_df = spark.createDataFrame(test_data, ["group", "item", "value"])
    
    print("\nTest Data:")
    test_df.show()
    
    # Test 1: Collect List preserves duplicates
    print("\n✓ Test 1: Collect List preserves duplicates")
    result1 = test_df.groupBy("group").agg(
        collect_list("item").alias("items"),
        size(collect_list("item")).alias("count")
    )
    result1.show(truncate=False)
    
    assert result1.filter(col("group") == "A").select("count").collect()[0][0] == 3, \
        "Collect list should preserve duplicates"
    print("  PASSED: Duplicates preserved")
    
    # Test 2: Collect Set removes duplicates
    print("\n✓ Test 2: Collect Set removes duplicates")
    result2 = test_df.groupBy("group").agg(
        collect_set("item").alias("items"),
        size(collect_set("item")).alias("count")
    )
    result2.show(truncate=False)
    
    assert result2.filter(col("group") == "A").select("count").collect()[0][0] == 2, \
        "Collect set should remove duplicates"
    print("  PASSED: Duplicates removed")
    
    # Test 3: Map creation
    print("\n✓ Test 3: Map from entries")
    result3 = test_df.groupBy("group").agg(
        map_from_entries(collect_set(struct("item", "value"))).alias("item_map")
    )
    result3.show(truncate=False)
    print("  PASSED: Map created successfully")
    
    # Test 4: Slice/Limit
    print("\n✓ Test 4: Slice limits collection size")
    result4 = test_df.groupBy("group").agg(
        slice(collect_list("item"), 1, 2).alias("limited_items"),
        size(slice(collect_list("item"), 1, 2)).alias("count")
    )
    result4.show(truncate=False)
    
    max_count = result4.agg(_max("count")).collect()[0][0]
    assert max_count <= 2, "Slice should limit collection size"
    print("  PASSED: Collection limited correctly")
    
    # Test 5: Empty collection handling
    print("\n✓ Test 5: Empty collection handling")
    empty_df = spark.createDataFrame([], "group STRING, item STRING, value INT")
    result5 = empty_df.groupBy("group").agg(
        collect_list("item").alias("items")
    )
    assert result5.count() == 0, "Empty input should produce empty output"
    print("  PASSED: Empty collections handled")
    
    # Test 6: Null handling
    print("\n✓ Test 6: Null value handling")
    null_data = [("A", None, 10), ("A", "item1", 20)]
    null_df = spark.createDataFrame(null_data, ["group", "item", "value"])
    result6 = null_df.groupBy("group").agg(
        collect_list("item").alias("items_with_null"),
        collect_set("item").alias("items_set")
    )
    result6.show(truncate=False)
    print("  PASSED: Nulls handled in collections")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ALL TESTS PASSED ✓")
    print("=" * 80)

def print_best_practices():
    """
    Prints comprehensive best practices for collection patterns.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("BEST PRACTICES GUIDE FOR COLLECTION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    best_practices = """
    
    1. CHOOSING THE RIGHT COLLECTION PATTERN
    ========================================
    
    Use collect_list when:
    ✓ Order matters
    ✓ Duplicates are meaningful
    ✓ You need to preserve all occurrences
    Example: Order history, event sequences
    
    Use collect_set when:
    ✓ Only unique values are needed
    ✓ Order doesn't matter
    ✓ Memory efficiency is important
    Example: Unique products, distinct categories
    
    Use map_from_entries when:
    ✓ You need key-value lookups
    ✓ Associating related data
    ✓ Building reference dictionaries
    Example: Product catalogs, configuration maps
    
    Use Top-N when:
    ✓ Only best/worst items needed
    ✓ Ranking is important
    ✓ Memory constraints exist
    Example: Top sellers, highest spenders
    
    Use Sample when:
    ✓ Representative subset needed
    ✓ Testing/validation required
    ✓ Exploratory analysis
    Example: A/B testing, data profiling
    
    Use Limited when:
    ✓ Preview/pagination needed
    ✓ Memory constraints exist
    ✓ Fixed-size outputs required
    Example: Recent items, first N records
    
    
    2. PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION
    ===========================
    
    Memory Management:
    ✓ Always limit collection size when possible
    ✓ Use collect_set instead of collect_list + distinct
    ✓ Avoid collect() on large datasets (use take() or limit())
    ✓ Monitor executor memory usage
    ✓ Use persist() for reused collections
    
    Computation Efficiency:
    ✓ Push filters before groupBy operations
    ✓ Use broadcast joins for small lookup tables
    ✓ Partition data appropriately
    ✓ Avoid unnecessary shuffles
    ✓ Use window functions for Top-N instead of sorting entire dataset
    
    Code Examples:
    
    # BAD: Collecting everything then filtering
    df.groupBy("id").agg(collect_list("value")).filter(size(col("value")) > 10)
    
    # GOOD: Filter first, then collect
    df.filter(col("value").isNotNull()).groupBy("id").agg(collect_list("value"))
    
    # BAD: Unlimited collection
    df.groupBy("id").agg(collect_list("value"))
    
    # GOOD: Limited collection
    df.groupBy("id").agg(slice(collect_list("value"), 1, 100))
    
    
    3. DATA QUALITY AND EDGE CASES
    ===============================
    
    Handle Nulls:
    ✓ Filter nulls before collection if not needed
    ✓ Use array_filter to remove nulls from collections
    ✓ Document null handling behavior
    
    Handle Empty Collections:
    ✓ Use coalesce or fillna for empty arrays
    ✓ Check collection size before processing
    ✓ Provide default values where appropriate
    
    Handle Duplicates:
    ✓ Choose collect_list vs collect_set appropriately
    ✓ Use distinct before collect_list if needed
    ✓ Document duplicate handling strategy
    
    
    4. SCALABILITY CONSIDERATIONS
    ==============================
    
    For Large Datasets:
    ✓ Use approximate algorithms when exact results not needed
    ✓ Implement pagination for large collections
    ✓ Use sampling for exploratory analysis
    ✓ Consider incremental processing
    ✓ Monitor and tune partition sizes
    
    For High Cardinality:
    ✓ Use Top-N instead of full collections
    ✓ Implement size limits per group
    ✓ Use bloom filters for existence checks
    ✓ Consider pre-aggregation strategies
    
    
    5. DEBUGGING AND MONITORING
    ===========================
    
    Add Metadata:
    ✓ Include collection sizes in output
    ✓ Add timestamps for temporal analysis
    ✓ Include counts and aggregates
    ✓ Log skewed partitions
    
    Validation:
    ✓ Check for unexpected nulls
    ✓ Validate collection sizes
    ✓ Monitor data skew
    ✓ Test with edge cases
    
    Example:
    df.groupBy("id").agg(
        collect_list("value").alias("values"),
        size(collect_list("value")).alias("value_count"),  # Add size
        count("*").alias("row_count")                       # Add count
    )
    
    
    6. EXPORT AND PERSISTENCE
    =========================
    
    Choose Format Based on Use Case:
    ✓ JSON: Complex nested structures, API consumption
    ✓ Parquet: Efficient storage, analytics workloads
    ✓ CSV: Business users, simple structures
    ✓ Avro: Schema evolution, streaming
    
    Optimize Exports:
    ✓ Partition output by relevant columns
    ✓ Coalesce small files
    ✓ Use compression appropriately
    ✓ Document schema and structure
    
    
    7. TESTING STRATEGIES
    =====================
    
    Unit Tests:
    ✓ Test with empty datasets
    ✓ Test with null values
    ✓ Test with duplicates
    ✓ Test with large collections
    ✓ Test edge cases (single item, all same values)
    
    Integration Tests:
    ✓ Test with realistic data volumes
    ✓ Test with actual data distributions
    ✓ Measure performance metrics
    ✓ Validate output correctness
    
    
    8. DOCUMENTATION
    ================
    
    Always Document:
    ✓ Why a specific pattern was chosen
    ✓ Size limits and their rationale
    ✓ Null handling behavior
    ✓ Performance characteristics
    ✓ Known limitations
    
    Example:
    # Collect top 100 products per customer (limited for memory efficiency)
    # Nulls are filtered out before collection
    # Results ordered by purchase date descending
    customer_products = df.filter(col("product").isNotNull()) \\
        .groupBy("customer_id") \\
        .agg(slice(collect_list("product"), 1, 100).alias("top_products"))
    
    
    9. COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
    ===========================
    
    ✗ Don't use collect() without limit on production data
    ✗ Don't ignore null values without handling
    ✗ Don't create unbounded collections
    ✗ Don't forget to unpersist cached data
    ✗ Don't use collect_list when collect_set suffices
    ✗ Don't sort entire dataset for Top-N (use window functions)
    ✗ Don't collect before filtering
    ✗ Don't ignore data skew in groupBy operations
    
    
    10. REAL-WORLD CHECKLIST
    ========================
    
    Before Deploying Collection Pattern Code:
    ☐ Estimated collection sizes per group?
    ☐ Memory requirements calculated?
    ☐ Null handling strategy defined?
    ☐ Size limits implemented?
    ☐ Performance tested with realistic data?
    ☐ Edge cases handled?
    ☐ Monitoring in place?
    ☐ Documentation complete?
    ☐ Fallback strategy for failures?
    ☐ Data quality checks implemented?
    
    """
    
    print(best_practices)

class CollectionPatternConfig:
    """
    Configuration class for collection pattern operations.
    Centralizes all configurable parameters.
    """
    
    # Memory and Performance Settings
    MAX_COLLECTION_SIZE = 1000
    DEFAULT_SAMPLE_FRACTION = 0.1
    DEFAULT_TOP_N = 10
    CACHE_ENABLED = True
    
    # Export Settings
    EXPORT_FORMAT = "parquet"  # Options: parquet, json, csv
    COMPRESSION = "snappy"
    PARTITION_COLUMNS = ["category"]
    
    # Quality Settings
    FILTER_NULLS = True
    REMOVE_DUPLICATES_IN_SET = True
    
    # Performance Tuning
    SHUFFLE_PARTITIONS = 200
    BROADCAST_THRESHOLD = 10 * 1024 * 1024  # 10MB
    
    @classmethod
    def apply_to_spark(cls, spark_session):
        """
        Apply configuration to Spark session.
        
        Args:
            spark_session: Active Spark session
        """
        spark_session.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", cls.SHUFFLE_PARTITIONS)
        spark_session.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", cls.BROADCAST_THRESHOLD)
        print(f"✓ Configuration applied to Spark session")
        print(f"  - Shuffle partitions: {cls.SHUFFLE_PARTITIONS}")
        print(f"  - Broadcast threshold: {cls.BROADCAST_THRESHOLD} bytes")


# ============================================================================
# Monitoring and Metrics
# ============================================================================

def collect_with_metrics(df, group_col, collect_col, pattern_type="list"):
    """
    Wrapper function that collects data while tracking metrics.
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        group_col: Column to group by
        collect_col: Column to collect
        pattern_type: Type of collection (list, set, map)
        
    Returns:
        tuple: (result DataFrame, metrics dict)
    """
    import time
    
    print(f"\n🔍 Collecting with metrics tracking...")
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # Perform collection based on pattern type
    if pattern_type == "list":
        result = df.groupBy(group_col).agg(
            collect_list(collect_col).alias("collected_values"),
            count("*").alias("row_count"),
            size(collect_list(collect_col)).alias("collection_size")
        )
    elif pattern_type == "set":
        result = df.groupBy(group_col).agg(
            collect_set(collect_col).alias("collected_values"),
            count("*").alias("row_count"),
            size(collect_set(collect_col)).alias("collection_size")
        )
    elif pattern_type == "map":
        result = df.groupBy(group_col).agg(
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(struct(collect_col, "value"))
            ).alias("collected_map"),
            count("*").alias("row_count")
        )
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown pattern type: {pattern_type}")
    
    # Force evaluation
    result.cache()
    total_groups = result.count()
    
    # Collect metrics
    metrics = {
        "pattern_type": pattern_type,
        "execution_time": time.time() - start_time,
        "total_groups": total_groups,
        "input_rows": df.count(),
        "timestamp": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
    }
    
    # Get collection size statistics if available
    if pattern_type in ["list", "set"]:
        size_stats = result.agg(
            _min("collection_size").alias("min_size"),
            _max("collection_size").alias("max_size"),
            avg("collection_size").alias("avg_size")
        ).collect()[0]
        
        metrics.update({
            "min_collection_size": size_stats["min_size"],
            "max_collection_size": size_stats["max_size"],
            "avg_collection_size": size_stats["avg_size"]
        })
    
    # Print metrics
    print("\n📊 Collection Metrics:")
    print("-" * 60)
    for key, value in metrics.items():
        if isinstance(value, float) and key != "timestamp":
            print(f"  {key}: {value:.2f}")
        else:
            print(f"  {key}: {value}")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    return result, metrics


# ============================================================================
# Advanced Patterns: Nested Collections
# ============================================================================

def nested_collection_patterns():
    """
    Demonstrates advanced nested collection patterns for complex hierarchical data.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED: NESTED COLLECTION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create hierarchical data
    hierarchical_data = [
        ("Region1", "Store1", "Electronics", "Laptop", 1200, 2),
        ("Region1", "Store1", "Electronics", "Mouse", 25, 5),
        ("Region1", "Store1", "Books", "Python Guide", 45, 3),
        ("Region1", "Store2", "Electronics", "Keyboard", 75, 4),
        ("Region2", "Store3", "Clothing", "T-Shirt", 20, 10),
        ("Region2", "Store3", "Clothing", "Jeans", 60, 5),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("region", StringType(), False),
        StructField("store", StringType(), False),
        StructField("category", StringType(), False),
        StructField("product", StringType(), False),
        StructField("price", DoubleType(), False),
        StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), False)
    ])
    
    hier_df = spark.createDataFrame(hierarchical_data, schema)
    
    print("\nHierarchical Data:")
    hier_df.show()
    
    # Pattern 1: Nested collections - Region > Store > Category > Products
    print("\n1. Multi-level Nested Collections:")
    
    nested_hierarchy = hier_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("region", "store", "category") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(
                struct("product", "price", "quantity", "revenue")
            ).alias("products")
        ) \
        .groupBy("region", "store") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(
                struct("category", "products")
            ).alias("categories")
        ) \
        .groupBy("region") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(
                struct("store", "categories")
            ).alias("stores")
        )
    
    print("Nested hierarchy (Region > Store > Category > Products):")
    nested_hierarchy.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 2: Nested maps
    print("\n2. Nested Map Collections:")
    
    nested_maps = hier_df \
        .groupBy("region", "store") \
        .agg(
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(
                    struct(
                        col("category"),
                        collect_list("product").alias("products")
                    )
                )
            ).alias("category_products_map")
        ) \
        .groupBy("region") \
        .agg(
            map_from_entries(
                collect_set(
                    struct("store", "category_products_map")
                )
            ).alias("store_hierarchy")
        )
    
    print("Nested map structure:")
    nested_maps.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 3: Mixed collections (arrays + maps)
    print("\n3. Mixed Collection Types:")
    
    mixed_collections = hier_df \
        .withColumn("revenue", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
        .groupBy("region") \
        .agg(
            # Array of stores
            collect_set("store").alias("stores"),
            # Map of category to total revenue
            map_from_entries(
                collect_list(
                    struct(
                        col("category"),
                        _sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue")
                    )
                )
            ).alias("category_revenue_map"),
            # Nested struct with arrays
            struct(
                collect_set("category").alias("all_categories"),
                collect_set("product").alias("all_products"),
                _sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue")
            ).alias("summary")
        )
    
    print("Mixed collection types:")
    mixed_collections.show(truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# Streaming Collection Patterns
# ============================================================================

def streaming_collection_patterns():
    """
    Demonstrates collection patterns for streaming data.
    Note: This is a simulation using batch processing.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("STREAMING COLLECTION PATTERNS (Simulated)")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Simulate streaming data with timestamps
    streaming_data = [
        ("2024-01-01 10:00:00", "C001", "P001", 100),
        ("2024-01-01 10:05:00", "C001", "P002", 150),
        ("2024-01-01 10:10:00", "C002", "P001", 100),
        ("2024-01-01 10:15:00", "C001", "P003", 200),
        ("2024-01-01 10:20:00", "C002", "P002", 150),
        ("2024-01-01 10:25:00", "C003", "P001", 100),
    ]
    
    stream_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        streaming_data,
        ["timestamp", "customer_id", "product_id", "amount"]
    ).withColumn("timestamp", col("timestamp").cast("timestamp"))
    
    print("\nSimulated Streaming Data:")
    stream_df.show()
    
    # Pattern 1: Windowed aggregation with collection
    print("\n1. Time-Windowed Collections:")
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import window
    
    windowed_collection = stream_df \
        .groupBy(
            window(col("timestamp"), "10 minutes"),
            "customer_id"
        ) \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_id").alias("products_in_window"),
            _sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
            count("*").alias("transaction_count")
        ) \
        .orderBy("window", "customer_id")
    
    print("Collections within time windows:")
    windowed_collection.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 2: Session-based collection
    print("\n2. Session-Based Collections:")
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    from pyspark.sql.functions import lag, unix_timestamp
    
    # Define session timeout (5 minutes = 300 seconds)
    session_timeout = 300
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("timestamp")
    
    sessions = stream_df \
        .withColumn("prev_timestamp", lag("timestamp").over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn(
            "time_diff",
            unix_timestamp("timestamp") - unix_timestamp("prev_timestamp")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "new_session",
            expr(f"CASE WHEN time_diff > {session_timeout} OR time_diff IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "session_id",
            _sum("new_session").over(
                Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("timestamp")
                .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
            )
        ) \
        .groupBy("customer_id", "session_id") \
        .agg(
            collect_list("product_id").alias("session_products"),
            _sum("amount").alias("session_total"),
            _min("timestamp").alias("session_start"),
            _max("timestamp").alias("session_end")
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id", "session_id")
    
    print("Session-based collections:")
    sessions.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 3: Sliding window collection
    print("\n3. Sliding Window Collections:")
    
    window_slide = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("timestamp") \
        .rowsBetween(-2, 0)  # Current and 2 previous rows
    
    sliding_collection = stream_df \
        .withColumn(
            "recent_products",
            collect_list("product_id").over(window_slide)
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "recent_total",
            _sum("amount").over(window_slide)
        ) \
        .select(
            "timestamp",
            "customer_id",
            "product_id",
            "amount",
            "recent_products",
            "recent_total"
        ) \
        .orderBy("customer_id", "timestamp")
    
    print("Sliding window collections:")
    sliding_collection.show(truncate=False)
