"""

class PredicateCodegenPattern:
    """
    Demonstrates predicate code generation for efficient filtering
    and conditional evaluation.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def create_customer_data(self):
        """Create sample customer and order data"""
        customers_schema = StructType([
            StructField("customer_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("age", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("income", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("credit_score", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("membership_level", StringType(), False),
            StructField("active", BooleanType(), False)
        ])
        
        orders_schema = StructType([
            StructField("order_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("customer_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("order_value", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("items_count", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("is_premium", BooleanType(), False)
        ])
        
        customers_data = [
            (i, 25 + (i % 50), 30000 + (i * 1000), 600 + (i % 250), 
             ["BRONZE", "SILVER", "GOLD", "PLATINUM"][i % 4],
             i % 3 != 0)
            for i in range(1, 10001)
        ]
        
        orders_data = [
            (i, (i % 10000) + 1, 50 + (i * 10), (i % 20) + 1, i % 2 == 0)
            for i in range(1, 50001)
        ]
        
        customers = self.spark.createDataFrame(customers_data, customers_schema)
        orders = self.spark.createDataFrame(orders_data, orders_schema)
        
        return customers, orders
    
    def demonstrate_complex_predicates(self):
        """
        Demonstrates predicate codegen with complex filtering conditions
        and join predicates.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("PATTERN 3: PREDICATE CODEGEN PATTERN")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        customers, orders = self.create_customer_data()
        
        # Complex predicate combinations
        # Multiple AND/OR conditions trigger predicate codegen
        filtered_customers = customers.filter(
            (
                (col("age").between(25, 45)) &
                (col("income") > 50000) &
                (col("credit_score") >= 700)
            ) |
            (
                (col("membership_level").isin(["GOLD", "PLATINUM"])) &
                (col("active") == True)
            )
        )
        
        # Complex join predicate
        result = filtered_customers.join(
            orders,
            (filtered_customers.customer_id == orders.customer_id) &
            (
                ((orders.order_value > 1000) & (orders.is_premium == True)) |
                (orders.items_count > 10)
            ),
            "inner"
        ).select(
            filtered_customers.customer_id,
            filtered_customers.age,
            filtered_customers.income,
            filtered_customers.membership_level,
            orders.order_value,
            orders.items_count,
            orders.is_premium
        ).filter(
            # Additional complex predicate after join
            (col("order_value") / col("income") < 0.5) &
            (col("items_count") > 5)
        )
        
        print("\nPredicate Plan (showing predicate pushdown and codegen):")
        print("-" * 80)
        result.explain(mode="formatted")
        
        print("\nFiltered Results:")
        print("-" * 80)
        result.show(10)
        
        # Show predicate statistics
        print("\nPredicate Selectivity Statistics:")
        print("-" * 80)
        print(f"Total customers: {customers.count()}")
        print(f"Filtered customers: {filtered_customers.count()}")
        print(f"Final result count: {result.count()}")
        
        return result

        result = df.select(

"""
Aggregate Codegen Pattern:
- Optimizes aggregation functions (sum, avg, count, etc.)
- Generates efficient hash-based aggregation code
- Handles multiple aggregations in single pass
- Optimizes memory usage for aggregation buffers
"""

class AggregateCodegenPattern:
    """
    Demonstrates aggregate code generation for efficient group-by
    and aggregation operations.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def create_sales_data(self):
        """Create comprehensive sales data for aggregation"""
        schema = StructType([
            StructField("sale_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("product_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("category", StringType(), False),
            StructField("subcategory", StringType(), False),
            StructField("region", StringType(), False),
            StructField("store_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("unit_price", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("discount", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("cost", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("sale_date", DateType(), False),
            StructField("year", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("quarter", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("month", IntegerType(), False)
        ])
        
        categories = ["Electronics", "Clothing", "Food", "Books", "Toys"]
        subcategories = {
            "Electronics": ["Phones", "Laptops", "Tablets"],
            "Clothing": ["Men", "Women", "Kids"],
            "Food": ["Groceries", "Snacks", "Beverages"],
            "Books": ["Fiction", "Non-Fiction", "Educational"],
            "Toys": ["Action", "Educational", "Outdoor"]
        }
        regions = ["North", "South", "East", "West", "Central"]
        
        data = []
        for i in range(1, 20001):
            category = categories[i % len(categories)]
            subcats = subcategories[category]
            
            data.append((
                i,
                1000 + (i % 500),
                category,
                subcats[i % len(subcats)],
                regions[i % len(regions)],
                100 + (i % 50),
                (i % 20) + 1,
                10.0 + (i % 100) * 5,
                0.05 + (i % 10) * 0.02,
                5.0 + (i % 50) * 2,
                f"2024-{((i % 12) + 1):02d}-{((i % 28) + 1):02d}",
                2024,
                ((i % 12) // 3) + 1,
                (i % 12) + 1
            ))
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    def demonstrate_complex_aggregations(self):
        """
        Demonstrates aggregate codegen with multiple aggregation functions,
        grouping sets, and window functions.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("PATTERN 5: AGGREGATE CODEGEN PATTERN")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        df = self.create_sales_data()
        
        # Add calculated columns for aggregation
        df_with_calcs = df.withColumn(
            "revenue",
            col("quantity") * col("unit_price") * (1 - col("discount"))
        ).withColumn(
            "profit",
            (col("quantity") * col("unit_price") * (1 - col("discount"))) - 
            (col("quantity") * col("cost"))
        ).withColumn(
            "profit_margin",
            col("profit") / (col("quantity") * col("unit_price"))
        )
        
        # Complex multi-level aggregation
        # Aggregate codegen optimizes multiple aggregations in single pass
        result = df_with_calcs.groupBy("category", "region", "quarter") \
            .agg(
                # Basic aggregations
                count("sale_id").alias("total_sales"),
                sum("quantity").alias("total_quantity"),
                sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
                sum("profit").alias("total_profit"),
                
                # Statistical aggregations
                avg("unit_price").alias("avg_unit_price"),
                stddev("unit_price").alias("stddev_price"),
                min("unit_price").alias("min_price"),
                max("unit_price").alias("max_price"),
                
                # Advanced aggregations
                avg("profit_margin").alias("avg_profit_margin"),
                percentile_approx("revenue", 0.5).alias("median_revenue"),
                countDistinct("product_id").alias("unique_products"),
                countDistinct("store_id").alias("unique_stores"),
                
                # Conditional aggregations
                sum(when(col("discount") > 0.1, col("revenue")).otherwise(0)).alias("discounted_revenue"),
                count(when(col("profit") > 0, 1)).alias("profitable_sales")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "profit_margin_pct",
                round((col("total_profit") / col("total_revenue")) * 100, 2)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "avg_sale_value",
                round(col("total_revenue") / col("total_sales"), 2)
            )
        
        print("\nAggregate Plan (showing hash aggregate codegen):")
        print("-" * 80)
        result.explain(mode="formatted")
        
        print("\nAggregation Results:")
        print("-" * 80)
        result.orderBy(desc("total_revenue")).show(15, truncate=False)
        
        # Advanced: Grouping Sets (ROLLUP)
        print("\nHierarchical Aggregation with ROLLUP:")
        print("-" * 80)
        rollup_result = df_with_calcs.rollup("category", "region") \
            .agg(
                sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
                sum("profit").alias("total_profit"),
                count("sale_id").alias("sale_count")
            ) \
            .orderBy("category", "region")
        
        rollup_result.show(20, truncate=False)
        
        # Advanced: CUBE aggregation
        print("\nMulti-dimensional Aggregation with CUBE:")
        print("-" * 80)
        cube_result = df_with_calcs.cube("category", "quarter") \
            .agg(
                sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
                avg("profit_margin").alias("avg_margin")
            ) \
            .orderBy("category", "quarter")
        
        cube_result.show(20, truncate=False)
        
        # Window aggregations (also use codegen)
        print("\nWindow Aggregations with Codegen:")
        print("-" * 80)
        from pyspark.sql.window import Window
        
        window_spec = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(desc("revenue"))
        
        window_result = df_with_calcs.groupBy("category", "product_id") \
            .agg(
                sum("revenue").alias("product_revenue"),
                sum("profit").alias("product_profit")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "rank",
                dense_rank().over(window_spec)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "running_total",
                sum("product_revenue").over(
                    window_spec.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
                )
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "pct_of_category",
                round((col("product_revenue") / sum("product_revenue").over(
                    Window.partitionBy("category")
                )) * 100, 2)
            ) \
            .filter(col("rank") <= 5)
        
        window_result.orderBy("category", "rank").show(25, truncate=False)
        
        return result

# PERFORMANCE COMPARISON AND BENCHMARKING
# ============================================================================

class CodegenBenchmark:
    """
    Benchmarks and compares performance with and without code generation.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def benchmark_codegen_impact(self):
        """
        Demonstrates the performance impact of code generation by comparing
        execution with codegen enabled vs disabled.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("CODE GENERATION PERFORMANCE BENCHMARK")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Create test data
        df = self.spark.range(0, 10000000).toDF("id") \
            .withColumn("value1", (col("id") % 1000).cast("double")) \
            .withColumn("value2", (col("id") % 500).cast("double")) \
            .withColumn("category", (col("id") % 10).cast("string"))
        
        # Complex query for benchmarking
        def complex_query(dataframe):
            return dataframe \
                .filter(col("value1") > 100) \
                .withColumn("computed", col("value1") * col("value2") / 100) \
                .groupBy("category") \
                .agg(
                    sum("computed").alias("total"),
                    avg("value1").alias("avg_val1"),
                    count("id").alias("count")
                ) \
                .orderBy(desc("total"))
        
        # Benchmark with codegen enabled
        print("\n1. WITH Whole-Stage Code Generation:")
        print("-" * 80)
        self.spark.conf.set("spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage", "true")
        
        start_time = time.time()
        result_with_codegen = complex_query(df)
        result_with_codegen.write.mode("overwrite").format("noop").save()
        time_with_codegen = time.time() - start_time
        
        print(f"Execution time: {time_with_codegen:.3f} seconds")
        result_with_codegen.explain(mode="formatted")
        result_with_codegen.show()
        
        # Benchmark with codegen disabled
        print("\n2. WITHOUT Whole-Stage Code Generation:")
        print("-" * 80)
        self.spark.conf.set("spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage", "false")
        
        start_time = time.time()
        result_without_codegen = complex_query(df)
        result_without_codegen.write.mode("overwrite").format("noop").save()
        time_without_codegen = time.time() - start_time
        
        print(f"Execution time: {time_without_codegen:.3f} seconds")
        result_without_codegen.explain(mode="formatted")
        result_without_codegen.show()
        
        # Performance comparison
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("PERFORMANCE COMPARISON")
        print("=" * 80)
        print(f"Time with codegen:    {time_with_codegen:.3f} seconds")
        print(f"Time without codegen: {time_without_codegen:.3f} seconds")
        
        if time_without_codegen > 0:
            speedup = time_without_codegen / time_with_codegen
            improvement = ((time_without_codegen - time_with_codegen) / time_without_codegen) * 100
            print(f"Speedup:              {speedup:.2f}x")
            print(f"Performance gain:     {improvement:.2f}%")
        
        # Re-enable codegen
        self.spark.conf.set("spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage", "true")

# ============================================================================
# ADVANCED CODE GENERATION UTILITIES
# ============================================================================

class CodegenAnalyzer:
    """
    Utility class to analyze and inspect code generation in Spark queries.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def analyze_query_codegen(self, dataframe, query_name="Query"):
        """
        Analyzes a DataFrame query to show code generation details.
        
        Args:
            dataframe: The DataFrame to analyze
            query_name: Name for the query being analyzed
        """
        print(f"\n{'=' * 80}")
        print(f"CODE GENERATION ANALYSIS: {query_name}")
        print(f"{'=' * 80}")
        
        # Show different explain modes
        print("\n1. SIMPLE PLAN:")
        print("-" * 80)
        dataframe.explain(mode="simple")
        
        print("\n2. EXTENDED PLAN:")
        print("-" * 80)
        dataframe.explain(mode="extended")
        
        print("\n3. CODEGEN PLAN:")
        print("-" * 80)
        dataframe.explain(mode="codegen")
        
        print("\n4. COST PLAN:")
        print("-" * 80)
        dataframe.explain(mode="cost")
        
        print("\n5. FORMATTED PLAN:")
        print("-" * 80)
        dataframe.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    def extract_codegen_stages(self, dataframe):
        """
        Extracts and counts WholeStageCodegen stages from a query plan.
        
        Args:
            dataframe: The DataFrame to analyze
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary with codegen statistics
        """
        plan = dataframe._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
        
        # Count WholeStageCodegen occurrences
        codegen_count = plan.count("WholeStageCodegen")
        
        # Extract stage information
        stats = {
            "total_codegen_stages": codegen_count,
            "has_codegen": codegen_count > 0,
            "plan_contains_project": "Project" in plan,
            "plan_contains_filter": "Filter" in plan,
            "plan_contains_aggregate": "HashAggregate" in plan,
            "plan_contains_sort": "Sort" in plan,
            "plan_contains_exchange": "Exchange" in plan
        }
        
        return stats
    
    def print_codegen_stats(self, stats):
        """
        Prints code generation statistics in a formatted way.
        
        Args:
            stats: Dictionary containing codegen statistics
        """
        print("\nCode Generation Statistics:")
        print("-" * 80)
        print(f"Total WholeStageCodegen stages: {stats['total_codegen_stages']}")
        print(f"Code generation enabled: {stats['has_codegen']}")
        print(f"Contains Project: {stats['plan_contains_project']}")
        print(f"Contains Filter: {stats['plan_contains_filter']}")
        print(f"Contains Aggregate: {stats['plan_contains_aggregate']}")
        print(f"Contains Sort: {stats['plan_contains_sort']}")
        print(f"Contains Exchange: {stats['plan_contains_exchange']}")

class RealWorldCodegenExamples:
    """
    Real-world examples demonstrating code generation patterns in practice.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.analyzer = CodegenAnalyzer(spark_session)
    
    def ecommerce_analytics_pipeline(self):
        """
        E-commerce analytics pipeline demonstrating multiple codegen patterns.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: E-COMMERCE ANALYTICS PIPELINE")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Create realistic e-commerce data
        orders_schema = StructType([
            StructField("order_id", LongType(), False),
            StructField("customer_id", LongType(), False),
            StructField("order_timestamp", TimestampType(), False),
            StructField("total_amount", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("discount_amount", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("shipping_cost", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("payment_method", StringType(), False),
            StructField("status", StringType(), False),
            StructField("device_type", StringType(), False)
        ])
        
        # Generate sample data
        from datetime import datetime, timedelta
        import random
        
        base_date = datetime(2024, 1, 1)
        payment_methods = ["CREDIT_CARD", "DEBIT_CARD", "PAYPAL", "CRYPTO"]
        statuses = ["COMPLETED", "PENDING", "CANCELLED", "REFUNDED"]
        devices = ["MOBILE", "DESKTOP", "TABLET"]
        
        orders_data = [
            (
                i,
                random.randint(1, 5000),
                base_date + timedelta(days=random.randint(0, 365)),
                random.uniform(20, 2000),
                random.uniform(0, 100),
                random.uniform(5, 50),
                random.choice(payment_methods),
                random.choice(statuses),
                random.choice(devices)
            )
            for i in range(1, 50001)
        ]
        
        orders = self.spark.createDataFrame(orders_data, orders_schema)
        
        # Complex analytics query using multiple codegen patterns
        analytics_result = orders \
            .filter(
                # Predicate codegen: complex filtering
                (col("status") == "COMPLETED") &
                (col("total_amount") > 50) &
                (year(col("order_timestamp")) == 2024)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                # Expression codegen: complex calculations
                "net_revenue",
                col("total_amount") - col("discount_amount")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "month",
                month(col("order_timestamp"))
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "revenue_category",
                when(col("net_revenue") < 100, "LOW")
                .when(col("net_revenue").between(100, 500), "MEDIUM")
                .when(col("net_revenue").between(500, 1000), "HIGH")
                .otherwise("PREMIUM")
            ) \
            .groupBy(
                # Aggregate codegen: multi-dimensional aggregation
                "payment_method",
                "device_type",
                "month",
                "revenue_category"
            ) \
            .agg(
                count("order_id").alias("order_count"),
                sum("net_revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
                avg("net_revenue").alias("avg_order_value"),
                sum("discount_amount").alias("total_discounts"),
                avg("shipping_cost").alias("avg_shipping"),
                countDistinct("customer_id").alias("unique_customers")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "avg_discount_pct",
                round((col("total_discounts") / (col("total_revenue") + col("total_discounts"))) * 100, 2)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "revenue_per_customer",
                round(col("total_revenue") / col("unique_customers"), 2)
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
        
        print("\nE-Commerce Analytics Query Plan:")
        self.analyzer.analyze_query_codegen(analytics_result, "E-Commerce Analytics")
        
        print("\nTop Revenue Segments:")
        analytics_result.show(20, truncate=False)
        
        # Extract and print codegen statistics
        stats = self.analyzer.extract_codegen_stats(analytics_result)
        self.analyzer.print_codegen_stats(stats)
        
        return analytics_result
    
    def financial_risk_analysis(self):
        """
        Financial risk analysis demonstrating expression and aggregate codegen.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: FINANCIAL RISK ANALYSIS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Create financial transactions data
        transactions_schema = StructType([
            StructField("transaction_id", LongType(), False),
            StructField("account_id", LongType(), False),
            StructField("amount", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("transaction_type", StringType(), False),
            StructField("merchant_category", StringType(), False),
            StructField("is_international", BooleanType(), False),
            StructField("risk_score", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("timestamp", TimestampType(), False)
        ])
        
        from datetime import datetime, timedelta
        import random
        
        base_time = datetime(2024, 1, 1)
        tx_types = ["PURCHASE", "WITHDRAWAL", "TRANSFER", "PAYMENT"]
        categories = ["RETAIL", "FOOD", "TRAVEL", "ENTERTAINMENT", "UTILITIES"]
        
        transactions_data = [
            (
                i,
                random.randint(1000, 9999),
                random.uniform(10, 10000),
                random.choice(tx_types),
                random.choice(categories),
                random.choice([True, False]),
                random.uniform(0, 100),
                base_time + timedelta(hours=random.randint(0, 8760))
            )
            for i in range(1, 100001)
        ]
        
        transactions = self.spark.createDataFrame(transactions_data, transactions_schema)
        
        # Complex risk analysis with multiple codegen patterns
        risk_analysis = transactions \
            .withColumn("hour", hour(col("timestamp"))) \
            .withColumn("day_of_week", dayofweek(col("timestamp"))) \
            .withColumn(
                # Expression codegen: complex risk scoring
                "adjusted_risk_score",
                when(col("is_international"), col("risk_score") * 1.5)
                .otherwise(col("risk_score"))
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "risk_tier",
                when(col("adjusted_risk_score") < 30, "LOW")
                .when(col("adjusted_risk_score").between(30, 60), "MEDIUM")
                .when(col("adjusted_risk_score").between(60, 80), "HIGH")
                .otherwise("CRITICAL")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "amount_category",
                when(col("amount") < 100, "MICRO")
                .when(col("amount").between(100, 1000), "SMALL")
                .when(col("amount").between(1000, 5000), "MEDIUM")
                .otherwise("LARGE")
            ) \
            .groupBy("account_id", "risk_tier", "merchant_category") \
            .agg(
                count("transaction_id").alias("transaction_count"),
                sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
                avg("amount").alias("avg_transaction"),
                max("adjusted_risk_score").alias("max_risk_score"),
                avg("adjusted_risk_score").alias("avg_risk_score"),
                sum(when(col("is_international"), 1).otherwise(0)).alias("intl_count"),
                countDistinct("transaction_type").alias("unique_tx_types")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "risk_weighted_exposure",
                col("total_amount") * (col("avg_risk_score") / 100)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "intl_transaction_pct",
                round((col("intl_count") / col("transaction_count")) * 100, 2)
            ) \
            .filter(col("transaction_count") > 5) \
            .orderBy(desc("risk_weighted_exposure"))
        
        print("\nFinancial Risk Analysis Query Plan:")
        self.analyzer.analyze_query_codegen(risk_analysis, "Risk Analysis")
        
        print("\nHigh-Risk Account Segments:")
        risk_analysis.show(20, truncate=False)
        
        # Additional analysis: Time-based patterns
        print("\nTime-Based Risk Patterns:")
        time_patterns = transactions \
            .withColumn("hour", hour(col("timestamp"))) \
            .withColumn(
                "time_period",
                when(col("hour").between(0, 6), "NIGHT")
                .when(col("hour").between(7, 12), "MORNING")
                .when(col("hour").between(13, 18), "AFTERNOON")
                .otherwise("EVENING")
            ) \
            .groupBy("time_period") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("tx_count"),
                avg("risk_score").alias("avg_risk"),
                sum(when(col("risk_score") > 70, 1).otherwise(0)).alias("high_risk_count")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "high_risk_pct",
                round((col("high_risk_count") / col("tx_count")) * 100, 2)
            )
        
        time_patterns.show()
        
        return risk_analysis
    
    def iot_sensor_analytics(self):
        """
        IoT sensor data analytics demonstrating projection and window codegen.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: IOT SENSOR ANALYTICS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Create IoT sensor data
        sensor_schema = StructType([
            StructField("sensor_id", StringType(), False),
            StructField("device_type", StringType(), False),
            StructField("location", StringType(), False),
            StructField("temperature", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("humidity", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("pressure", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("battery_level", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("signal_strength", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("timestamp", TimestampType(), False)
        ])
        
        from datetime import datetime, timedelta
        import random
        
        base_time = datetime(2024, 1, 1)
        devices = ["TEMP_SENSOR", "WEATHER_STATION", "SMART_METER"]
        locations = ["ZONE_A", "ZONE_B", "ZONE_C", "ZONE_D"]
        
        sensor_data = [
            (
                f"SENSOR_{i % 100:03d}",
                random.choice(devices),
                random.choice(locations),
                random.uniform(15, 35),
                random.uniform(30, 80),
                random.uniform(980, 1020),
                random.
```python
                random.uniform(20, 100),
                random.randint(-90, -30),
                base_time + timedelta(minutes=i)
            )
            for i in range(1, 100001)
        ]
        
        sensors = self.spark.createDataFrame(sensor_data, sensor_schema)
        
        # Complex IoT analytics with window functions and codegen
        from pyspark.sql.window import Window
        
        # Define window specifications
        sensor_window = Window.partitionBy("sensor_id").orderBy("timestamp")
        location_window = Window.partitionBy("location").orderBy("timestamp")
        
        iot_analytics = sensors \
            .withColumn(
                # Expression codegen: complex sensor calculations
                "heat_index",
                col("temperature") + (0.5555 * (6.11 * exp(5417.7530 * ((1/273.16) - (1/(col("temperature") + 273.15)))) - 10))
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "sensor_health_score",
                (col("battery_level") * 0.4) + 
                ((col("signal_strength") + 90) / 60 * 100 * 0.6)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "anomaly_score",
                when(
                    (col("temperature") > 30) | 
                    (col("humidity") > 70) | 
                    (col("battery_level") < 30),
                    100
                ).when(
                    (col("temperature") > 28) | 
                    (col("humidity") > 65) | 
                    (col("battery_level") < 50),
                    50
                ).otherwise(0)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                # Window codegen: moving averages
                "temp_moving_avg",
                avg("temperature").over(
                    sensor_window.rowsBetween(-5, 0)
                )
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "humidity_moving_avg",
                avg("humidity").over(
                    sensor_window.rowsBetween(-5, 0)
                )
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                # Window codegen: lag for change detection
                "temp_change",
                col("temperature") - lag("temperature", 1).over(sensor_window)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                # Window codegen: ranking
                "sensor_rank",
                dense_rank().over(
                    Window.partitionBy("location").orderBy(desc("sensor_health_score"))
                )
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "reading_number",
                row_number().over(sensor_window)
            )
        
        # Aggregate analytics
        summary_analytics = iot_analytics \
            .groupBy("location", "device_type") \
            .agg(
                count("sensor_id").alias("reading_count"),
                countDistinct("sensor_id").alias("active_sensors"),
                avg("temperature").alias("avg_temperature"),
                stddev("temperature").alias("temp_stddev"),
                avg("humidity").alias("avg_humidity"),
                avg("sensor_health_score").alias("avg_health_score"),
                sum(when(col("anomaly_score") > 50, 1).otherwise(0)).alias("anomaly_count"),
                max("heat_index").alias("max_heat_index"),
                min("battery_level").alias("min_battery")
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "anomaly_rate",
                round((col("anomaly_count") / col("reading_count")) * 100, 2)
            ) \
            .withColumn(
                "health_status",
                when(col("avg_health_score") > 70, "GOOD")
                .when(col("avg_health_score").between(40, 70), "FAIR")
                .otherwise("POOR")
            )
        
        print("\nIoT Sensor Analytics Query Plan:")
        self.analyzer.analyze_query_codegen(iot_analytics, "IoT Analytics")
        
        print("\nSensor Summary by Location and Device Type:")
        summary_analytics.orderBy("location", "device_type").show(20, truncate=False)
        
        # Alert detection
        print("\nCritical Sensor Alerts:")
        alerts = iot_analytics \
            .filter(
                (col("anomaly_score") >= 50) |
                (col("sensor_health_score") < 40) |
                (abs(col("temp_change")) > 5)
            ) \
            .select(
                "sensor_id",
                "location",
                "device_type",
                "temperature",
                "temp_change",
                "battery_level",
                "sensor_health_score",
                "anomaly_score",
                "timestamp"
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("anomaly_score"), "timestamp")
        
        alerts.show(15, truncate=False)
        
        return iot_analytics, summary_analytics

# CODEGEN OPTIMIZATION TIPS AND BEST PRACTICES
# ============================================================================

class CodegenBestPractices:
    """
    Demonstrates best practices and optimization tips for code generation.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def demonstrate_best_practices(self):
        """
        Shows best practices for maximizing code generation benefits.
        """
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("CODE GENERATION BEST PRACTICES")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Create sample data
        df = self.spark.range(0, 1000000).toDF("id") \
            .withColumn("value", (col("id") % 1000).cast("double"))
        
        print("\n1. AVOID UDFs - Use Built-in Functions")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("❌ BAD: Using UDF (disables codegen)")
        
        # UDF example (BAD - disables codegen)
        from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
        from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
        
        @udf(returnType=DoubleType())
        def calculate_with_udf(value):
            return value * 2 + 10
        
        bad_result = df.withColumn("result", calculate_with_udf(col("value")))
        print("Plan with UDF:")
        bad_result.explain()
        
        print("\n✓ GOOD: Using built-in functions (enables codegen)")
        good_result = df.withColumn("result", col("value") * 2 + 10)
        print("Plan with built-in functions:")
        good_result.explain()
        
        print("\n2. CHAIN OPERATIONS FOR WHOLE-STAGE CODEGEN")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("✓ GOOD: Chained operations get fused into single stage")
        
        chained_result = df \
            .filter(col("value") > 100) \
            .withColumn("computed1", col("value") * 2) \
            .withColumn("computed2", col("computed1") + 100) \
            .withColumn("computed3", col("computed2") / 3) \
            .filter(col("computed3") < 1000)
        
        chained_result.explain()
        
        print("\n3. USE NATIVE TYPES")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("✓ GOOD: Native types (Int, Double, String) optimize better")
        
        native_types = df.select(
            col("id").cast("int").alias("id_int"),
            col("value").cast("double").alias("value_double"),
            col("id").cast("string").alias("id_string")
        )
        
        print("\n4. MINIMIZE DATA SHUFFLING")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("✓ GOOD: Reduce shuffles to maintain codegen stages")
        
        # Efficient aggregation
        efficient_agg = df \
            .withColumn("category", (col("id") % 10).cast("string")) \
            .groupBy("category") \
            .agg(
                sum("value").alias("total"),
                count("id").alias("count")
            )
        
        efficient_agg.explain()
        
        print("\n5. USE COLUMN PRUNING")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("✓ GOOD: Select only needed columns early")
        
        # Create wider dataset
        wide_df = df
        for i in range(10):
            wide_df = wide_df.withColumn(f"col_{i}", col("value") + i)
        
        # Prune early
        pruned = wide_df.select("id", "value", "col_0", "col_1") \
            .filter(col("value") > 500)
        
        print("Pruned columns early - better codegen")
        pruned.explain()
        
        print("\n6. LEVERAGE PREDICATE PUSHDOWN")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("✓ GOOD: Filter early in the pipeline")
        
        filtered_early = df \
            .filter(col("value") > 500) \
            .withColumn("computed", col("value") * 2) \
            .groupBy((col("id") % 10).cast("string").alias("group")) \
            .agg(sum("computed").alias("total"))
        
        filtered_early.explain()
        
        print("\n7. BATCH COLUMN ADDITIONS")
        print("-" * 80)
        print("✓ GOOD: Add multiple columns in single operation when possible")
        
        batched = df.selectExpr(
            "id",
            "value",
            "value * 2 as doubled",
            "value + 100 as added",
            "value / 2 as halved"
        )
        
        batched.explain()
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("CONFIGURATION RECOMMENDATIONS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        recommendations = {
            "spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage": "true (Enable whole-stage codegen)",
            "spark.sql.codegen.maxFields": "100-200 (Balance compilation time vs performance)",
            "spark.sql.codegen.factoryMode": "FALLBACK (Use fallback for safety)",
            "spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit": "65535 (Default, increase if needed)",
            "spark.sql.codegen.splitConsumeFuncByOperator": "true (Better for complex queries)",
            "spark.sql.codegen.methodSplitThreshold": "1024 (Adjust based on query complexity)"
        }
        
        for config, description in recommendations.items():
            print(f"{config:50s} : {description}")

## 1. Sort Order Pattern

```python
"""
Sort Order Pattern - Basic sorting with ascending/descending order
Use Case: Simple sorting of data by one or more columns
"""

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, desc, asc
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType, DoubleType

def sort_order_pattern():
    """
    Demonstrates basic sort operations in PySpark
    - Ascending and descending sorts
    - Single and multiple column sorts
    - Null handling in sorts
    """
    
    # Initialize Spark Session
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("SortOrderPattern") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    # Create sample data
    data = [
        ("Alice", "Sales", 85000, 5),
        ("Bob", "Engineering", 95000, 3),
        ("Charlie", "Sales", 75000, 7),
        ("David", "Engineering", 105000, 8),
        ("Eve", "Marketing", 70000, 2),
        ("Frank", None, 80000, 4),  # Null department
        ("Grace", "Sales", None, 6)  # Null salary
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("name", StringType(), True),
        StructField("department", StringType(), True),
        StructField("salary", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("years_experience", IntegerType(), True)
    ])
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print("SORT ORDER PATTERN EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Simple ascending sort
    print("\n1. Ascending Sort by Salary:")
    df.orderBy("salary").show()
    
    # Example 2: Descending sort
    print("\n2. Descending Sort by Salary:")
    df.orderBy(desc("salary")).show()
    
    # Example 3: Multiple column sort
    print("\n3. Sort by Department (asc) then Salary (desc):")
    df.orderBy(col("department").asc(), col("salary").desc()).show()
    
    # Example 4: Null handling - nulls first
    print("\n4. Sort with Nulls First:")
    df.orderBy(col("salary").asc_nulls_first()).show()
    
    # Example 5: Null handling - nulls last
    print("\n5. Sort with Nulls Last:")
    df.orderBy(col("salary").asc_nulls_last()).show()
    
    # Example 6: Using sort() - alias for orderBy
    print("\n6. Using sort() method:")
    df.sort(col("years_experience").desc()).show()
    
    # Example 7: Complex multi-column sort
    print("\n7. Complex Multi-Column Sort:")
    df.orderBy(
        col("department").asc_nulls_last(),
        col("salary").desc_nulls_last(),
        col("name").asc()
    ).show()
    
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sort_order_pattern()

## 2. Partial Order Pattern

```python
"""
Partial Order Pattern - Sorting within partitions
Use Case: Maintain order within logical groups without global ordering
Performance: More efficient than total order for large datasets
"""

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, row_number, rank, dense_rank
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType, DateType
from datetime import date

def partial_order_pattern():
    """
    Demonstrates partial ordering within partitions
    - Partition-based sorting
    - Window functions with ordering
    - Top-N within groups
    """
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("PartialOrderPattern") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    # Create sample sales data
    data = [
        ("Electronics", "Laptop", 1200, date(2024, 1, 15), "Store-A"),
        ("Electronics", "Mouse", 25, date(2024, 1, 16), "Store-A"),
        ("Electronics", "Keyboard", 75, date(2024, 1, 17), "Store-B"),
        ("Clothing", "Shirt", 45, date(2024, 1, 15), "Store-A"),
        ("Clothing", "Pants", 65, date(2024, 1, 16), "Store-B"),
        ("Clothing", "Jacket", 120, date(2024, 1, 17), "Store-A"),
        ("Books", "Novel", 15, date(2024, 1, 15), "Store-B"),
        ("Books", "Textbook", 95, date(2024, 1, 16), "Store-A"),
        ("Electronics", "Monitor", 350, date(2024, 1, 18), "Store-B"),
        ("Clothing", "Shoes", 85, date(2024, 1, 18), "Store-A")
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("category", StringType(), True),
        StructField("product", StringType(), True),
        StructField("price", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("sale_date", DateType(), True),
        StructField("store", StringType(), True)
    ])
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print("PARTIAL ORDER PATTERN EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Sort within partitions
    print("\n1. Sort Within Partitions by Category:")
    df.repartition("category") \
        .sortWithinPartitions("price") \
        .show()
    
    # Example 2: Window function with partition ordering
    print("\n2. Rank Products Within Each Category:")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(col("price").desc())
    
    df.withColumn("rank", rank().over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("dense_rank", dense_rank().over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("row_num", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .show()
    
    # Example 3: Top-N per partition
    print("\n3. Top 2 Most Expensive Products per Category:")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(col("price").desc())
    
    df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .filter(col("rank") <= 2) \
        .orderBy("category", "rank") \
        .show()
    
    # Example 4: Multiple partition keys with ordering
    print("\n4. Sort Within Category and Store Partitions:")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("category", "store").orderBy(col("sale_date"))
    
    df.withColumn("sale_sequence", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .orderBy("category", "store", "sale_sequence") \
        .show()
    
    # Example 5: Partition-wise cumulative operations
    print("\n5. Running Total Within Each Category:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("category") \
        .orderBy("sale_date") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    df.withColumn("running_total", _sum("price").over(window_spec)) \
        .orderBy("category", "sale_date") \
        .show()
    
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    partial_order_pattern()
```

## 3. Total Order Pattern

```python
"""
Total Order Pattern - Global ordering across all partitions
Use Case: When complete dataset ordering is required
Note: Expensive operation for large datasets due to single partition collection
"""

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, monotonically_increasing_id, spark_partition_id
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType, TimestampType
from datetime import datetime

def total_order_pattern():
    """
    Demonstrates total ordering patterns
    - Global sorting across all partitions
    - Coalesce for single partition ordering
    - Techniques to maintain global order
    """
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("TotalOrderPattern") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    # Create sample event log data
    data = [
        ("User-101", "login", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 30, 0)),
        ("User-102", "page_view", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 31, 0)),
        ("User-101", "click", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 32, 0)),
        ("User-103", "login", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 33, 0)),
        ("User-102", "purchase", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 34, 0)),
        ("User-101", "logout", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 35, 0)),
        ("User-103", "click", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 36, 0)),
        ("User-104", "login", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 37, 0)),
        ("User-102", "logout", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 38, 0)),
        ("User-103", "purchase", datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 39, 0))
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("user_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("event_type", StringType(), True),
        StructField("timestamp", TimestampType(), True)
    ])
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print("TOTAL ORDER PATTERN EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Basic total order
    print("\n1. Total Order by Timestamp (Global Sort):")
    df.orderBy("timestamp").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Show partition distribution before ordering
    print("\n2. Partition Distribution Before Total Order:")
    df.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .groupBy("partition_id").count() \
        .show()
    
    # Example 3: Total order with coalesce (for smaller datasets)
    print("\n3. Total Order with Single Partition (Coalesce):")
    ordered_df = df.orderBy("timestamp").coalesce(1)
    
    ordered_df.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .withColumn("global_order", monotonically_increasing_id()) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 4: Range partitioning for better total order performance
    print("\n4. Total Order with Range Partitioning:")
    # repartitionByRange maintains order within partitions
    df.repartitionByRange(2, "timestamp") \
        .sortWithinPartitions("timestamp") \
        .withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 5: Multiple column total order
    print("\n5. Multi-Column Total Order:")
    df.orderBy(col("user_id").asc(), col("timestamp").asc()) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 6: Total order with limit (optimized)
    print("\n6. Top-K Global Ordering (Optimized):")
    # Using limit with orderBy is optimized in Spark
    df.orderBy(col("timestamp").desc()) \
        .limit(5) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 7: Demonstrating cost of total order
    print("\n7. Analyzing Total Order Performance:")
    print("Number of partitions before orderBy:", df.rdd.getNumPartitions())
    ordered_df = df.orderBy("timestamp")
    print("Number of partitions after orderBy:", ordered_df.rdd.getNumPartitions())
    
    # Show the execution plan
    print("\nExecution Plan for Total Order:")
    ordered_df.explain(mode="simple")
    
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    total_order_pattern()
```

```python
"""
Range Order Pattern - Ordering data within specific ranges
Use Case: Bucketing data into ranges and ordering within/across ranges
Useful for: Time-series analysis, histogram generation, percentile calculations
"""

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, when, lit, ntile, floor
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType, DoubleType
import sys

def range_order_pattern():
    """
    Demonstrates range-based ordering patterns
    - Bucketing into ranges
    - Ordering within ranges
    - Range partitioning strategies
    """
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("RangeOrderPattern") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    # Create sample customer transaction data
    data = [
        ("C001", "Alice", 150.50, 25),
        ("C002", "Bob", 2500.00, 35),
        ("C003", "Charlie", 450.75, 28),
        ("C004", "David", 8500.00, 45),
        ("C005", "Eve", 125.00, 22),
        ("C006", "Frank", 3200.00, 38),
        ("C007", "Grace", 750.00, 31),
        ("C008", "Henry", 15000.00, 52),
        ("C009", "Iris", 95.50, 19),
        ("C010", "Jack", 5500.00, 42),
        ("C011", "Kate", 320.00, 27),
        ("C012", "Leo", 12000.00, 48),
        ("C013", "Mia", 680.00, 33),
        ("C014", "Noah", 210.00, 24),
        ("C015", "Olivia", 4200.00, 40)
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("customer_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("name", StringType(), True),
        StructField("transaction_amount", DoubleType(), True),
        StructField("age", IntegerType(), True)
    ])
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print("RANGE ORDER PATTERN EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Define custom ranges and order within them
```python
    # Example 1: Define custom ranges and order within them
    print("\n1. Custom Amount Ranges with Ordering:")
    df_with_ranges = df.withColumn(
        "amount_range",
        when(col("transaction_amount") < 500, "Low (0-500)")
        .when((col("transaction_amount") >= 500) & (col("transaction_amount") < 2000), "Medium (500-2000)")
        .when((col("transaction_amount") >= 2000) & (col("transaction_amount") < 5000), "High (2000-5000)")
        .otherwise("Premium (5000+)")
    )
    
    df_with_ranges.orderBy("amount_range", col("transaction_amount").desc()) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Age range bucketing with ordering
    print("\n2. Age Range Bucketing:")
    df_age_ranges = df.withColumn(
        "age_group",
        when(col("age") < 25, "18-24")
        .when((col("age") >= 25) & (col("age") < 35), "25-34")
        .when((col("age") >= 35) & (col("age") < 45), "35-44")
        .otherwise("45+")
    )
    
    df_age_ranges.orderBy("age_group", col("transaction_amount").desc()) \
        .show()
    
    # Example 3: Percentile-based ranges (quartiles)
    print("\n3. Quartile-Based Range Ordering:")
    window_spec = Window.orderBy("transaction_amount")
    
    df_quartiles = df.withColumn("quartile", ntile(4).over(window_spec))
    
    df_quartiles.orderBy("quartile", col("transaction_amount")) \
        .show()
    
    # Example 4: Range partitioning by specific column
    print("\n4. Range Partitioning by Transaction Amount:")
    # repartitionByRange creates range-based partitions
    df_range_partitioned = df.repartitionByRange(3, "transaction_amount")
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import spark_partition_id
    df_range_partitioned.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .orderBy("partition_id", "transaction_amount") \
        .show()
    
    # Example 5: Dynamic range calculation with ordering
    print("\n5. Dynamic Percentile Ranges:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import percent_rank
    
    window_spec = Window.orderBy("transaction_amount")
    
    df.withColumn("percentile_rank", percent_rank().over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn(
            "percentile_range",
            when(col("percentile_rank") < 0.25, "Bottom 25%")
            .when(col("percentile_rank") < 0.50, "25-50%")
            .when(col("percentile_rank") < 0.75, "50-75%")
            .otherwise("Top 25%")
        ) \
        .orderBy("percentile_range", col("transaction_amount")) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 6: Fixed-width range bucketing
    print("\n6. Fixed-Width Range Bucketing ($2000 buckets):")
    bucket_width = 2000
    
    df.withColumn(
        "bucket",
        floor(col("transaction_amount") / bucket_width) * bucket_width
    ).withColumn(
        "bucket_label",
        when(col("bucket") == 0, "$0-$2000")
        .when(col("bucket") == 2000, "$2000-$4000")
        .when(col("bucket") == 4000, "$4000-$6000")
        .when(col("bucket") == 6000, "$6000-$8000")
        .otherwise("$8000+")
    ).orderBy("bucket", col("transaction_amount")) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 7: Range-based aggregation with ordering
    print("\n7. Aggregated Statistics per Range:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import count, avg, min as _min, max as _max
    
    df_with_ranges.groupBy("amount_range") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("customer_count"),
            avg("transaction_amount").alias("avg_amount"),
            _min("transaction_amount").alias("min_amount"),
            _max("transaction_amount").alias("max_amount")
        ) \
        .orderBy("min_amount") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    spark.stop()

        # Priority scoring
        priority_scores = {"Critical": 100, "High": 75, "Medium": 50, "Low": 25}
        score += priority_scores.get(priority, 0)
        
        # Status scoring (earlier stages get higher priority)
        status_scores = {"Open": 20, "In Progress": 15, "In Review": 10, "Testing": 5, "Done": 0}
        score += status_scores.get(status, 0)
        
        # Task type scoring
        type_scores = {"Bug Fix": 30, "Feature": 20, "Enhancement": 15, "Documentation": 5}
        score += type_scores.get(task_type, 0)
        
        return score
    
    # Register UDF
    priority_score_udf = udf(calculate_priority_score, IntegerType())
    
    df.withColumn(
        "priority_score",
        priority_score_udf(col("priority"), col("status"), col("task_type"))
    ).orderBy(col("priority_score").desc(), col("created_date")) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 6: Day-of-week custom ordering
    print("\n6. Custom Day-of-Week Ordering (Mon-Sun):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import dayofweek
    
    # dayofweek returns 1=Sunday, 2=Monday, ..., 7=Saturday
    # Reorder to start with Monday
    df.withColumn("day_of_week", dayofweek(col("created_date"))) \
        .withColumn(
            "custom_day_order",
            when(col("day_of_week") == 1, 7)  # Sunday -> 7
            .otherwise(col("day_of_week") - 1)  # Monday=1, ..., Saturday=6
        ) \
        .orderBy("custom_day_order", "created_date") \
        .drop("day_of_week", "custom_day_order") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 7: Alphabetical with exceptions
    print("\n7. Alphabetical Ordering with Priority Exceptions:")
    # Order alphabetically but keep "Critical" tasks first
    
    df.withColumn(
        "sort_key",
        when(col("priority") == "Critical", lit("AAA_" + col("task_id")))
        .otherwise(col("task_id"))
    ).orderBy("sort_key") \
        .drop("sort_key") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    custom_order_pattern()
```

## 6. Multi-Column Order Pattern

```python
"""
Multi-Column Order Pattern - Complex ordering across multiple columns
Use Case: Hierarchical sorting, composite keys, complex business requirements
"""

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, desc, asc, coalesce, concat_ws, struct
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType, DoubleType, DateType
from datetime import date

def multi_column_order_pattern():
    """
    Demonstrates multi-column ordering patterns
    - Hierarchical ordering
    - Mixed ascending/descending ordering
    - Null handling in multi-column sorts
    - Complex composite ordering
    """
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("MultiColumnOrderPattern") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    # Create sample employee data with multiple attributes
    data = [
        ("Engineering", "Software", "Senior", "Alice", 95000, 5, date(2019, 3, 15)),
        ("Engineering", "Software", "Junior", "Bob", 65000, 1, date(2023, 1, 10)),
        ("Engineering", "Hardware", "Senior", "Charlie", 92000, 6, date(2018, 7, 20)),
        ("Sales", "Enterprise", "Senior", "David", 88000, 7, date(2017, 5, 12)),
        ("Sales", "Enterprise", "Mid", "Eve", 72000, 3, date(2021, 9, 8)),
        ("Sales", "SMB", "Junior", "Frank", 58000, 2, date(2022, 2, 14)),
        ("Engineering", "Software", "Mid", "Grace", 78000, 3, date(2021, 11, 5)),
        ("Marketing", "Digital", "Senior", "Henry", 82000, 5, date(2019, 6, 22)),
        ("Marketing", "Digital", "Mid", "Iris", 68000, 2, date(2022, 4, 18)),
        ("Engineering", None, "Senior", "Jack", 90000, 4, None),  # Null sub-department
        ("
```python
        ("Engineering", None, "Senior", "Jack", 90000, 4, None),  # Null sub-department
        ("Sales", "SMB", "Senior", "Kate", 85000, 8, date(2016, 12, 3)),
        ("Marketing", "Content", "Junior", "Leo", 55000, 1, date(2023, 3, 7)),
        ("Engineering", "Software", "Senior", "Mia", 98000, 6, date(2018, 8, 30)),
        ("Sales", "Enterprise", "Mid", "Noah", 75000, 4, date(2020, 10, 25)),
        ("Marketing", "Digital", "Senior", "Olivia", 84000, 5, date(2019, 2, 16))
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("department", StringType(), True),
        StructField("sub_department", StringType(), True),
        StructField("level", StringType(), True),
        StructField("name", StringType(), True),
        StructField("salary", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("years_experience", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("hire_date", DateType(), True)
    ])
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print("MULTI-COLUMN ORDER PATTERN EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Basic multi-column ordering
    print("\n1. Basic Multi-Column Sort (Dept ASC, Salary DESC):")
    df.orderBy(
        col("department").asc(),
        col("salary").desc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 2: Hierarchical ordering (3 levels)
    print("\n2. Hierarchical Ordering (Dept > Sub-Dept > Level):")
    df.orderBy(
        col("department").asc(),
        col("sub_department").asc_nulls_last(),
        col("level").desc()  # Senior > Mid > Junior
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 3: Mixed ascending/descending with custom level order
    print("\n3. Mixed Order with Custom Level Ranking:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import when
    
    df.withColumn(
        "level_rank",
        when(col("level") == "Senior", 1)
        .when(col("level") == "Mid", 2)
        .when(col("level") == "Junior", 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    ).orderBy(
        col("department").asc(),
        col("level_rank").asc(),
        col("salary").desc()
    ).drop("level_rank") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 4: Multi-column with null handling
    print("\n4. Multi-Column Sort with Null Handling:")
    df.orderBy(
        col("department").asc(),
        col("sub_department").asc_nulls_last(),
        col("hire_date").asc_nulls_last(),
        col("name").asc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 5: Complex business logic ordering
    print("\n5. Complex Business Logic Ordering:")
    # Order by: Department, then by seniority (experience + level), then by performance (salary)
    
    df.withColumn(
        "level_weight",
        when(col("level") == "Senior", 10)
        .when(col("level") == "Mid", 5)
        .otherwise(0)
    ).withColumn(
        "seniority_score",
        col("years_experience") + col("level_weight")
    ).orderBy(
        col("department").asc(),
        col("seniority_score").desc(),
        col("salary").desc()
    ).drop("level_weight", "seniority_score") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 6: Composite key ordering
    print("\n6. Composite Key Ordering:")
    # Create composite key from multiple columns
    
    df.withColumn(
        "composite_key",
        concat_ws("_", col("department"), coalesce(col("sub_department"), lit("NONE")), col("level"))
    ).orderBy(
        col("composite_key").asc(),
        col("salary").desc()
    ).drop("composite_key") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 7: Struct-based ordering
    print("\n7. Struct-Based Multi-Column Ordering:")
    # Using struct for cleaner multi-column ordering
    
    df.orderBy(
        struct(
            col("department").asc(),
            col("sub_department").asc_nulls_last(),
            col("salary").desc()
        )
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 8: Window function with multi-column ordering
    print("\n8. Ranking with Multi-Column Order Criteria:")
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    from pyspark.sql.functions import rank, dense_rank, row_number
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(
        col("level").asc(),
        col("years_experience").desc(),
        col("salary").desc()
    )
    
    df.withColumn("dept_rank", rank().over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("dept_dense_rank", dense_rank().over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("dept_row_num", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .orderBy("department", "dept_rank") \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 9: Multi-column ordering with aggregations
    print("\n9. Aggregated Data with Multi-Column Ordering:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import count, avg, sum as _sum, max as _max
    
    df.groupBy("department", "level") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("employee_count"),
            avg("salary").alias("avg_salary"),
            _max("years_experience").alias("max_experience")
        ) \
        .orderBy(
            col("department").asc(),
            col("avg_salary").desc(),
            col("employee_count").desc()
        ) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 10: Dynamic multi-column ordering
    print("\n10. Dynamic Multi-Column Ordering (Configurable):")
    
    # Define ordering configuration
    order_config = [
        ("department", "asc"),
        ("sub_department", "asc"),
        ("salary", "desc"),
        ("name", "asc")
    ]
    
    # Build ordering dynamically
    order_cols = []
    for col_name, direction in order_config:
        if direction.lower() == "desc":
            order_cols.append(col(col_name).desc())
        else:
            order_cols.append(col(col_name).asc())
    
    df.orderBy(*order_cols).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 11: Multi-column ordering with computed columns
    print("\n11. Ordering by Computed Columns:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import datediff, current_date
    
    df.withColumn(
        "tenure_days",
        datediff(current_date(), coalesce(col("hire_date"), current_date()))
    ).withColumn(
        "salary_per_year_exp",
        col("salary") / (col("years_experience") + 1)  # Avoid division by zero
    ).orderBy(
        col("department").asc(),
        col("tenure_days").desc(),
        col("salary_per_year_exp").desc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 12: Optimized multi-column ordering for large datasets
    print("\n12. Optimized Multi-Column Ordering (with repartition):")
    
    # For large datasets, repartition by primary sort key first
    optimized_df = df.repartition("department") \
        .sortWithinPartitions(
            col("department").asc(),
            col("salary").desc(),
            col("years_experience").desc()
        )
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import spark_partition_id
    optimized_df.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .show(truncate=False)
    
    # Example 13: Case-insensitive multi-column ordering
    print("\n13. Case-Insensitive Multi-Column Ordering:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import lower
    
    df.orderBy(
        lower(col("department")).asc(),
        lower(col("name")).asc(),
        col("salary").desc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    multi_column_order_pattern()
```

        ("ORD-015", "CUST-111", "Express", "Processing", 680.00, datetime(2024, 1, 15, 9, 25), "Home", "US-West")

        StructField("order_id", StringType(), True),

        StructField("status", StringType(), True),
        StructField("order_amount", DoubleType(), True),
        StructField("order_timestamp", TimestampType(), True),
        StructField("category", StringType(), True),
        StructField("region", StringType(), True)

    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE ORDERING EXAMPLE: E-COMMERCE ORDER PROCESSING")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Scenario 1: Warehouse Fulfillment Priority
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 1: Warehouse Fulfillment Priority ===")
    print("Order processing queue based on shipping tier, status, and order time\n")
    
    # Custom ordering: Express > Premium > Standard
    # Status: Pending > Processing > Shipped > Delivered
    # Then by order time (oldest first)
    
    fulfillment_df = df.withColumn(
        "tier_priority",
        when(col("shipping_tier") == "Express", 1)
        .when(col("shipping_tier") == "Premium", 2)
        .otherwise(3)
    ).withColumn(
        "status_priority",
        when(col("status") == "Pending", 1)
        .when(col("status") == "Processing", 2)
        .when(col("status") == "Shipped", 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    )
    
    fulfillment_df.orderBy(
        col("tier_priority").asc(),
        col("status_priority").asc(),
        col("order_timestamp").asc()
    ).select(
        "order_id", "shipping_tier", "status", "order_amount",

    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 2: Regional Processing (Partial Order Pattern)
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 2: Regional Processing Queues ===")
    print("Orders grouped by region with internal prioritization\n")
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("region").orderBy(
        col("tier_priority").asc(),
        col("order_amount").desc()
    )
    
    df.withColumn(
        "tier_priority",
        when(col("shipping_tier") == "Express", 1)
        .when(col("shipping_tier") == "Premium", 2)
        .otherwise(3)
    ).withColumn(
        "regional_queue_position",
        row_number().over(window_spec)
    ).orderBy("region", "regional_queue_position") \
        .select(
            "region", "regional_queue_position", "order_id", 
            "shipping
```python
            "shipping_tier", "order_amount", "status"
        ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 3: Revenue-Based Priority (Range Order Pattern)
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 3: Revenue-Based Order Segmentation ===")
    print("Orders categorized by value ranges for different processing teams\n")
    
    revenue_df = df.withColumn(
        "value_segment",
        when(col("order_amount") < 100, "Low Value ($0-$100)")
        .when((col("order_amount") >= 100) & (col("order_amount") < 500), "Medium Value ($100-$500)")
        .when((col("order_amount") >= 500) & (col("order_amount") < 1500), "High Value ($500-$1500)")
        .otherwise("Premium Value ($1500+)")
    ).withColumn(
        "segment_priority",
        when(col("order_amount") >= 1500, 1)
        .when(col("order_amount") >= 500, 2)
        .when(col("order_amount") >= 100, 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    )
    
    revenue_df.orderBy(
        col("segment_priority").asc(),
        col("order_amount").desc()
    ).select(
        "value_segment", "order_id", "order_amount", 
        "shipping_tier", "status"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 4: Customer Loyalty Analysis (Multi-Column Order)
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 4: Customer Loyalty Analysis ===")
    print("Customer ranking by order count and total spend\n")
    
    customer_summary = df.groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            count("order_id").alias("order_count"),
            sum("order_amount").alias("total_spent"),
            max("order_timestamp").alias("last_order_date"),
            avg("order_amount").alias("avg_order_value")
        )
    
    # Multi-column ordering: Most orders, highest spend, most recent activity
    customer_summary.orderBy(
        col("order_count").desc(),
        col("total_spent").desc(),
        col("last_order_date").desc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 5: Category Performance (Total Order with Aggregation)
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 5: Category Performance Ranking ===")
    print("Product categories ranked by total revenue and order volume\n")
    
    category_performance = df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            count("order_id").alias("total_orders"),
            sum("order_amount").alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("order_amount").alias("avg_order_value"),
            countDistinct("customer_id").alias("unique_customers")
        )
    
    category_performance.orderBy(
        col("total_revenue").desc(),
        col("total_orders").desc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 6: Time-Based Processing Windows (Custom Order)
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 6: Time-Based Processing Windows ===")
    print("Orders grouped by processing time windows with priority\n")
    
    time_window_df = df.withColumn(
        "hour_of_day",
        hour(col("order_timestamp"))
    ).withColumn(
        "processing_window",
        when(col("hour_of_day").between(8, 11), "Morning Batch (8AM-11AM)")
        .when(col("hour_of_day").between(12, 15), "Afternoon Batch (12PM-3PM)")
        .when(col("hour_of_day").between(16, 19), "Evening Batch (4PM-7PM)")
        .otherwise("Off-Hours")
    ).withColumn(
        "window_priority",
        when(col("hour_of_day").between(8, 11), 1)
        .when(col("hour_of_day").between(12, 15), 2)
        .when(col("hour_of_day").between(16, 19), 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    )
    
    time_window_df.orderBy(
        col("window_priority").asc(),
        col("order_timestamp").asc()
    ).select(
        "processing_window", "order_id", "order_timestamp", 
        "shipping_tier", "order_amount"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 7: Composite Business Priority Score
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 7: Composite Business Priority Scoring ===")
    print("Advanced scoring combining multiple business factors\n")
    
    # Complex business logic combining multiple factors
    priority_scored_df = df.withColumn(
        "tier_score",
        when(col("shipping_tier") == "Express", 50)
        .when(col("shipping_tier") == "Premium", 30)
        .otherwise(10)
    ).withColumn(
        "status_score",
        when(col("status") == "Pending", 40)
        .when(col("status") == "Processing", 30)
        .when(col("status") == "Shipped", 10)
        .otherwise(0)
    ).withColumn(
        "value_score",
        when(col("order_amount") >= 1000, 30)
        .when(col("order_amount") >= 500, 20)
        .when(col("order_amount") >= 100, 10)
        .otherwise(5)
    ).withColumn(
        "age_hours",
        (unix_timestamp(current_timestamp()) - unix_timestamp(col("order_timestamp"))) / 3600
    ).withColumn(
        "urgency_score",
        when(col("age_hours") > 24, 20)
        .when(col("age_hours") > 12, 15)
        .when(col("age_hours") > 6, 10)
        .otherwise(5)
    ).withColumn(
        "total_priority_score",
        col("tier_score") + col("status_score") + col("value_score") + col("urgency_score")
    )
    
    priority_scored_df.orderBy(col("total_priority_score").desc()) \
        .select(
            "order_id", "total_priority_score", "shipping_tier", 
            "status", "order_amount", "age_hours"
        ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 8: Optimized Batch Processing (Range Partitioning)
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 8: Optimized Batch Processing ===")
    print("Range-partitioned orders for parallel processing\n")
    
    # Use range partitioning for efficient distributed processing
    partitioned_df = df.repartitionByRange(3, "order_amount")
    
    partitioned_df.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .orderBy("partition_id", col("order_amount").desc()) \
        .select(
            "partition_id", "order_id", "order_amount", 
            "category", "region"
        ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 9: SLA Compliance Monitoring
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 9: SLA Compliance Monitoring ===")
    print("Orders at risk of missing SLA deadlines\n")
    
    sla_df = df.withColumn(
        "sla_hours",
        when(col("shipping_tier") == "Express", 24)
        .when(col("shipping_tier") == "Premium", 48)
        .otherwise(72)
    ).withColumn(
        "hours_since_order",
        (unix_timestamp(current_timestamp()) - unix_timestamp(col("order_timestamp"))) / 3600
    ).withColumn(
        "hours_remaining",
        col("sla_hours") - col("hours_since_order")
    ).withColumn(
        "sla_status",
        when(col("hours_remaining") < 0, "OVERDUE")
        .when(col("hours_remaining") < 6, "CRITICAL")
        .when(col("hours_remaining") < 12, "WARNING")
        .otherwise("ON_TRACK")
    ).withColumn(
        "sla_priority",
        when(col("sla_status") == "OVERDUE", 1)
        .when(col("sla_status") == "CRITICAL", 2)
        .when(col("sla_status") == "WARNING", 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    )
    
    sla_df.filter(col("status").isin(["Pending", "Processing"])) \
        .orderBy(
            col("sla_priority").asc(),
            col("hours_remaining").asc()
        ).select(
            "order_id", "sla_status", "hours_remaining", 
            "shipping_tier", "status", "order_amount"
        ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Scenario 10: Executive Dashboard Summary
    print("\n=== SCENARIO 10: Executive Dashboard Summary ===")
    print("High-level metrics with multi-dimensional ordering\n")
    
    executive_summary = df.groupBy("region", "category", "shipping_tier") \
        .agg(
            count("order_id").alias("order_count"),
            sum("order_amount").alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("order_amount").alias("avg_order_value"),
            min("order_timestamp").alias("first_order"),
            max("order_timestamp").alias("last_order")
        )
    
    executive_summary.orderBy(
        col("total_revenue").desc(),
        col("region").asc(),
        col("category").asc()
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Performance Insights
    print("\n=== PERFORMANCE INSIGHTS ===")
    print("\nExecution Plan for Complex Ordering:")
    priority_scored_df.orderBy(col("total_priority_score").desc()).explain(mode="formatted")
    
    print("\nOptimization Tips:")
    print("1. Use sortWithinPartitions() for partition-local ordering")
    print("2. Use repartitionByRange() for ordered data distribution")
    print("3. Avoid orderBy() followed by coalesce(1) on large datasets")
    print("4. Consider bucketing for frequently ordered columns")
    print("5. Use window functions instead of self-joins with ordering")
    
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
